daa-c1-t01.title: Algorithm: Definition
daa-c1-t01.definition: An algorithm is a finite, well-defined sequence of steps that takes some input and produces the required output for solving a problem.
daa-c1-t01.simpleExplanation: Algorithm ek step-by-step recipe hai jo input leke output deta hai aur kabhi na khatam hone wala loop nahi hota. Program us recipe ka code form hai.
daa-c1-t01.realLifeAnalogy: A cooking recipe: ingredients are input, steps are the algorithm, and the dish is the output.
daa-c1-t01.example: Find the largest number in [3, 9, 4]: set max=3; compare 9>3 → max=9; compare 4>9? no; output 9.
keyPoints: Algorithm ≠ program: algorithm is language independent; program is its implementation.
Has input, output, finite steps and each step is clear.
One problem can have many algorithms; we choose the most efficient.
Described using natural language, flowchart or pseudocode.
Correctness + efficiency are the key quality measures.
Time and space are the main resources analysed.
commonMistakes: Calling any code an algorithm even if it may not terminate.
Mixing the algorithm (idea) with its program (implementation).

examQuestions.question: Define algorithm.
examQuestions.answer: A finite sequence of well-defined steps that transforms input into output to solve a problem.

examQuestions.question: Algorithm vs program.
examQuestions.answer: Algorithm is language-independent logic; program is its code in a language.

examQuestions.question: Can a problem have more than one algorithm?
examQuestions.answer: Yes; e.g. sorting has many (bubble, merge, quick).

knowledgeCheck.question: An algorithm depends on programming language.
Name three ways to express an algorithm.
Two sorting methods give same output but different speed. What differs?
What are the main measures of an algorithm?

daa-c1-t01.quickRevision: Algorithm = finite, well-defined steps: input → output; language-independent; judged by correctness, time, space.
daa-c1-t01.problemStatement: Find the maximum of n numbers.
daa-c1-t01.approach: Scan once keeping the largest seen so far.
algorithmSteps: 1. Set max = A[1].
2. For i = 2 to n: if A[i] > max then max = A[i].
3. Return max.
daa-c1-t01.pseudocode:
Algorithm Max(A, n)
  max ← A[1]
  for i ← 2 to n do
    if A[i] > max then max ← A[i]
  return max
daa-c1-t01.workedExample: A=[3,9,4]: max=3 → 9>3 so max=9 → 4>9 false → output 9.

daa-c1-t02.title: Properties of Algorithms
daa-c1-t02.definition: An algorithm must satisfy: input, output, definiteness, finiteness and effectiveness (and should be correct and general).
daa-c1-t02.simpleExplanation: Algorithm ke 5 zaroori gun: input (0 ya zyada), output (kam se kam 1), definiteness (har step saaf), finiteness (khatam ho), effectiveness (step simple aur doable).
daa-c1-t02.realLifeAnalogy: A good recipe: clear steps, finishes in reasonable time, every step is something a cook can actually do.
daa-c1-t02.example: Euclid's GCD(48,18): 48 mod 18 = 12; 18 mod 12 = 6; 12 mod 6 = 0 → GCD = 6. Inputs 48,18; output 6; each step is definite and doable; it terminates because the remainder decreases.
keyPoints: Input: zero or more externally supplied values.
Output: at least one result.
Definiteness: each step is precise and unambiguous.
Finiteness: terminates after a finite number of steps.
Effectiveness: every step is basic enough to be carried out exactly.
Also desirable: correctness, generality, efficiency.
ifYouKnow: Say why a loop without exit violates them.
commonMistakes: Treating 'infinite loop' procedures as algorithms.
Using vague steps like 'make it fast' (not definite).

examQuestions.question: Explain properties of an algorithm.
examQuestions.answer: Input, output, definiteness, finiteness, effectiveness with example.

examQuestions.question: Which property does 'while true' violate?
examQuestions.answer: Finiteness.

knowledgeCheck.question: An algorithm may have zero outputs.
What is definiteness?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Each step is clear and unambiguous.

knowledgeCheck.question: Instruction 'pick a good number' — which property fails?

daa-c1-t02.quickRevision: Properties: input, output, definiteness, finiteness, effectiveness (+correctness).
algorithmSteps: 1. While b ≠ 0: r = a mod b; a = b; b = r.
2. Return a.
daa-c1-t02.pseudocode:
Algorithm GCD(a, b)
  while b ≠ 0 do
    r ← a mod b
    a ← b
    b ← r
  return a

daa-c1-t03.title: Types of Algorithms
daa-c1-t03.definition: Algorithms can be classified by design approach (brute force, divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming, backtracking, branch and bound, randomised) and by other features such as recursive/iterative and exact/approximate.
daa-c1-t03.simpleExplanation: Algorithms ko design style ke hisaab se types me baanta jata hai: brute force, divide & conquer, greedy, dynamic programming, backtracking, etc. Har type ka alag use hota hai.
daa-c1-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Different ways to travel: walk everywhere (brute force), split the route among friends (D&C), always take the nearest road (greedy).
daa-c1-t03.example: Sorting: bubble sort (brute force), merge sort (divide & conquer). Shortest path: Dijkstra (greedy), Floyd–Warshall (dynamic programming). N-Queens: backtracking.
keyPoints: Brute force: try all possibilities.
Divide and conquer: split, solve, combine (merge sort).
Greedy: best local choice each step (Kruskal).
Dynamic programming: store sub-problem results (LCS).
Backtracking: build solution and undo on failure (N-Queens).
Branch and bound: prune using bounds (TSP).
Randomised, approximation, recursive vs iterative, serial vs parallel.
ifYouKnow: Choose a type for a problem.
commonMistakes: Calling every recursive algorithm divide and conquer.
Using greedy where optimal substructure + greedy-choice property fails.

examQuestions.question: Explain different types of algorithms with examples.
examQuestions.answer: Brute force, D&C, greedy, DP, backtracking, B&B, randomised.

examQuestions.question: Greedy vs dynamic programming.
examQuestions.answer: Greedy commits to a local best choice; DP considers all sub-problems and stores results.

knowledgeCheck.question: Overlapping sub-problems and optimal substructure. Technique?
Exact vs approximation algorithms.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Exact gives optimal; approximation gives near-optimal in polynomial time.

daa-c1-t03.quickRevision: Types: brute force, D&C, greedy, DP, backtracking, B&B, randomised; recursive/iterative; exact/approx.

daa-c1-t04.title: Writing an Algorithm
daa-c1-t04.definition: Writing an algorithm means expressing the solution steps clearly using natural language, a flowchart or pseudocode with defined inputs, outputs and control structures.
daa-c1-t04.simpleExplanation: Algorithm likhte waqt input/output pehle define karo, steps clear aur numbered likho, aur pseudocode me loops/conditions use karo. Pseudocode kisi bhi language me convert ho sakta hai.
daa-c1-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Writing a recipe card: list ingredients, then numbered steps anyone can follow.
daa-c1-t04.example: Linear search: input A[1..n], key; output index or −1. Pseudocode below. For A=[4,7,9], key=9 → returns 3.
keyPoints: State problem, input and output first.
Use consistent notation: ← for assignment, indentation for blocks.
Control structures: sequence, if/else, for, while, repeat–until.
Use meaningful variable names and comments.
Avoid language-specific syntax in pseudocode.
Dry-run on sample input to verify.
ifYouKnow: Write pseudocode for a simple task.
commonMistakes: Mixing assignment and equality (← vs =).
Skipping input/output specification.

examQuestions.question: Write pseudocode for linear search.
examQuestions.answer: Loop through array comparing with key; return index or −1.

examQuestions.question: Why pseudocode instead of code?
examQuestions.answer: It is language independent and focuses on logic.

knowledgeCheck.question: Algorithms need defined input and output.
Symbol used for assignment in pseudocode?
Verifying an algorithm on sample data is called?

daa-c1-t04.quickRevision: Write: define I/O → numbered steps → pseudocode (← , indentation) → dry-run.
daa-c1-t04.problemStatement: Search for key in array A[1..n].
algorithmSteps: 1. For i = 1 to n: if A[i] = key return i.
2. Return −1.
daa-c1-t04.pseudocode:
Algorithm LinearSearch(A, n, key)
  for i ← 1 to n do
    if A[i] = key then return i
  return −1

daa-c1-t05.title: Algorithm Analysis: Parameters
daa-c1-t05.definition: Algorithm analysis predicts the resources an algorithm uses, mainly time complexity and space complexity as functions of input size n.
daa-c1-t05.simpleExplanation: Analysis ka matlab hai algorithm kitna time aur memory lega, input size n ke function ke roop me. Isse alag algorithms ko compare kar sakte hain.
daa-c1-t05.realLifeAnalogy: Comparing two routes by time and fuel needed for a given distance.
daa-c1-t05.example: Sum of n numbers: loop executes n times. Count ≈ n additions + constant ⇒ T(n)=n+c ⇒ O(n). Space: one variable sum ⇒ O(1).
keyPoints: Main parameters: time complexity and space complexity.
Other criteria: correctness, simplicity, optimality, generality.
Input size n is the measure; basic operation is counted.
A priori analysis (theoretical, machine independent) vs a posteriori (experimental, machine dependent).
RAM model assumes each basic operation takes constant time.
Growth rate matters for large n, not constants.
commonMistakes: Measuring only wall-clock time (machine dependent).
Ignoring space complexity.

examQuestions.question: Explain parameters of algorithm analysis.
examQuestions.answer: Time, space, plus correctness etc.; a priori vs a posteriori.

examQuestions.question: A priori vs a posteriori analysis.
examQuestions.answer: A priori: mathematical, machine independent; a posteriori: runs the code and measures.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the input size n?
knowledgeCheck.answer: The quantity describing the problem size, e.g. number of elements.

knowledgeCheck.question: Loop runs n times with 1 op each. T(n)?

daa-c1-t05.quickRevision: Analysis: time & space vs input size n; a priori (theory) vs a posteriori (experiment); count basic operations.
daa-c1-t05.timeComplexity: Counted as number of basic operations T(n)
daa-c1-t05.workedExample: for i=1..n: sum←sum+A[i] → n additions → T(n)=n → O(n).

daa-c1-t06.title: Design Techniques of Algorithms
daa-c1-t06.definition: Design techniques are general strategies for building algorithms: brute force, divide and conquer, greedy, dynamic programming, backtracking and branch and bound.
daa-c1-t06.simpleExplanation: Design technique ek general approach hai jisse hum bahut saare problems solve karte hain. Problem ki nature dekh ke technique chunte hain.
daa-c1-t06.realLifeAnalogy: Like having a toolbox: hammer, screwdriver, wrench; choose the tool by the job.
daa-c1-t06.example: Problem: find shortest paths. Single source with nonnegative weights → greedy (Dijkstra). All pairs → dynamic programming (Floyd–Warshall). Maximum non-overlapping meetings → greedy (activity selection).
keyPoints: Brute force: simple but slow.
Divide & conquer: sub-problems independent (merge sort).
Greedy: needs greedy-choice property + optimal substructure.
Dynamic programming: overlapping sub-problems + optimal substructure.
Backtracking: search with pruning of infeasible partial solutions.
Branch & bound: optimisation with bounds to prune.
Choice depends on problem structure.
commonMistakes: Using DP when sub-problems are independent (D&C fits).
Using greedy without proving the greedy choice.

examQuestions.question: Explain algorithm design techniques.
examQuestions.answer: Each with idea and example.

examQuestions.question: Divide & conquer vs dynamic programming.
examQuestions.answer: D&C: independent sub-problems; DP: overlapping sub-problems stored and reused.

knowledgeCheck.question: Merge two halves after solving separately. Technique?
Backtracking vs branch & bound.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Backtracking: feasibility search; B&B: optimisation with bounds.

daa-c1-t06.quickRevision: Techniques: brute force, D&C, greedy, DP, backtracking, B&B; choose by problem structure.

daa-c1-t07.title: Asymptotic Notations: Big Oh, Big Omega & Big Theta
daa-c1-t07.definition: Asymptotic notations describe the growth rate of a function for large n: Big Oh (upper bound), Big Omega (lower bound) and Big Theta (tight bound).
daa-c1-t07.simpleExplanation: Asymptotic notation batata hai n bahut bada hone par function kitni tezi se badhta hai. O = upper limit, Ω = lower limit, Θ = dono (tight).
daa-c1-t07.realLifeAnalogy: Speed limits: O = 'not faster than' a maximum, Ω = 'at least' a minimum, Θ = exactly in this range.
keyPoints: f(n)=O(g(n)) if ∃ c>0, n0: f(n) ≤ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
f(n)=Ω(g(n)) if f(n) ≥ c·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0.
f(n)=Θ(g(n)) if c1·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c2·g(n) ∀ n ≥ n0 (both O and Ω).
Growth order: 1 < log n < n < n log n < n² < n³ < 2ⁿ < n!.
Drop constants and lower-order terms.
Little-o and little-ω denote strict bounds.
commonMistakes: Saying O is the exact complexity (that is Θ).
Forgetting to give c and n0 in proofs.

examQuestions.question: Show 3n+2 = Θ(n).
examQuestions.answer: 3n ≤ 3n+2 ≤ 4n for n ≥ 2 ⇒ Θ(n).

examQuestions.question: Define Big O, Ω, Θ.
examQuestions.answer: As above with c and n0.

examQuestions.question: Is n² = O(n³)?
examQuestions.answer: Yes, O is an upper bound (not tight).

knowledgeCheck.question: Order n log n vs n².
O vs Ω.
knowledgeCheck.answer: O upper bound; Ω lower bound.

daa-c1-t07.quickRevision: O: f≤c·g (upper); Ω: f≥c·g (lower); Θ: both (tight); drop constants; 1<log n<n<n log n<n²<2ⁿ<n!.

daa-c1-t08.title: Lower Bound, Upper Bound and Tight Bound
daa-c1-t08.definition: An upper bound limits how large the running time can be (O), a lower bound limits how small it can be (Ω), and a tight bound (Θ) is both.
daa-c1-t08.simpleExplanation: Upper bound = maximum itna time lagega, lower bound = kam se kam itna lagega, tight bound = ye dono same ho. Algorithm aur problem dono ke bounds hote hain.
daa-c1-t08.realLifeAnalogy: Travel time Delhi–Jaipur: 'at most 6 hours' (upper), 'at least 3 hours' (lower), '4–5 hours typical' (tight).
daa-c1-t08.example: Insertion sort: worst case Θ(n²), best case Θ(n). Any comparison-based sorting problem needs Ω(n log n) comparisons, so merge sort (Θ(n log n)) is asymptotically optimal.
keyPoints: Upper bound O(g): running time never exceeds g (for large n).
Lower bound Ω(g): running time is at least g.
Tight bound Θ(g): both.
Bounds can describe an algorithm or a problem.
Problem lower bound: comparison sorting is Ω(n log n).
An algorithm matching the problem's lower bound is optimal.
ifYouKnow: Decide if an algorithm is optimal.
commonMistakes: Confusing upper bound of an algorithm with lower bound of a problem.
Calling any O-bound tight.

examQuestions.question: Explain lower, upper and tight bounds with example.
examQuestions.answer: Definitions plus insertion sort case bounds.

examQuestions.question: Is merge sort optimal for comparison sorting?
examQuestions.answer: Yes; Θ(n log n) matches Ω(n log n).

knowledgeCheck.question: A tight bound is both O and Ω.
When is an algorithm optimal?
knowledgeCheck.answer: When its upper bound equals the problem's lower bound.

knowledgeCheck.question: Algorithm takes O(n²) but problem needs Ω(n log n). Optimal?
Upper vs lower bound.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Upper: at most; lower: at least.

daa-c1-t08.quickRevision: Upper = O (at most), lower = Ω (at least), tight = Θ; comparison sorting needs Ω(n log n).

daa-c1-t09.title: Best Case, Worst Case, Average Case
daa-c1-t09.definition: Best, worst and average case analyses give the minimum, maximum and expected running time of an algorithm over inputs of size n.
daa-c1-t09.simpleExplanation: Same size ke alag inputs par algorithm alag speed se chalta hai. Best = sabse tez input, worst = sabse dheema, average = expected.
daa-c1-t09.realLifeAnalogy: Searching for a book on a shelf: best case it's the first book; worst case it's the last or missing; average is somewhere in the middle.
daa-c1-t09.example: Linear search over n elements: best 1 comparison (key at first), worst n (last/absent), average (1+2+…+n)/n=(n+1)/2 if key present and equally likely at any position.
keyPoints: Best case: minimum steps (often not very useful).
Worst case: maximum steps — gives a guarantee; most commonly used.
Average case: expected steps over all inputs (needs a probability assumption).
Quick sort: best/average Θ(n log n), worst Θ(n²).
Insertion sort: best Θ(n), worst Θ(n²).
Big-O usually states the worst case.
ifYouKnow: Compute the three cases for linear search.
commonMistakes: Assuming average = (best+worst)/2 always.
Using best case to claim efficiency.

examQuestions.question: Average comparisons in linear search with n=10.
Explain best, worst and average case.
examQuestions.answer: Definitions with linear search example.

knowledgeCheck.question: Worst case gives an upper guarantee.
Best vs worst case.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Best minimal work; worst maximal work.

daa-c1-t09.quickRevision: Best (min), worst (max, used for guarantees), average (expected); linear search 1, n, (n+1)/2.
daa-c1-t09.workedExample: A=[5,8,2,9], key=2 → 3 comparisons; key=5 → 1 (best); key=7 → 4 (worst, absent).
daa-c1-t09.timeComplexity: Linear search: best O(1), average O(n), worst O(n)

daa-c1-t10.title: Analyzing Control Statements
daa-c1-t10.definition: Analysing control statements means computing the running time of sequences, conditionals and loops (single, nested, dependent, logarithmic) by counting executions.
daa-c1-t10.simpleExplanation: Time nikalne ke liye har control statement ka cost jodte hain: sequence me add, if me max branch, loop me (iterations × body cost). Nested loops multiply.
daa-c1-t10.realLifeAnalogy: Counting laps: one loop of n laps costs n; a loop inside a loop costs n × n.
daa-c1-t10.example: for i=1..n { for j=1..n { x++ } } → n² times. for(i=1;i<n;i=i*2) → about log₂ n times. for i=1..n { for j=1..i } → 1+2+…+n = n(n+1)/2 = Θ(n²).
keyPoints: Sequence: add costs.
if/else: cost of condition + max(branch costs) for worst case.
Single loop: n × body cost.
Nested independent loops: multiply.
Dependent inner loop: sum the series (e.g. n(n+1)/2).
Loop with i←i×2 or i←i/2 runs ⌊log₂ n⌋+1 times.
commonMistakes: Treating dependent nested loops as n×n exactly (it is n(n+1)/2, still Θ(n²)).
Missing that doubling loops are logarithmic.

examQuestions.question: Complexity of for(i=1;i<=n;i*=2) for(j=1;j<=n;j++).
examQuestions.answer: log n × n = O(n log n).

knowledgeCheck.question: Nested loops multiply iteration counts when independent.
if-else with branches costing n and n². Worst-case cost?

daa-c1-t10.quickRevision: Control statements: sequence add; if max; loops multiply; dependent loops n(n+1)/2; i*=2 → log n.
algorithmSteps: 1. Identify each statement's cost.
2. Sequence: add; conditional: max branch; loop: iterations × body.
3. For nested loops, count the innermost executions as a sum.
4. Keep the dominant term.
daa-c1-t10.workedExample: for i=1..n { for j=1..i { print } } → Σ i = n(n+1)/2 ⇒ Θ(n²).

daa-c1-t11.title: Loop Invariant and Correctness of Algorithms
daa-c1-t11.definition: A loop invariant is a condition that is true before and after each iteration of a loop; proving initialisation, maintenance and termination shows the algorithm correct.
daa-c1-t11.simpleExplanation: Loop invariant ek aisi shart hai jo har iteration ke pehle aur baad sach rehti hai. Teen cheezein prove karte hain: shuru me sach (initialization), har iteration me sach rehti hai (maintenance), end me useful result deti hai (termination).
daa-c1-t11.realLifeAnalogy: Like a checkpoint rule on a journey: you remain on the right route after each stop, so at the end you reach the destination.
daa-c1-t11.example: Insertion sort: invariant — at the start of iteration j, A[1..j−1] is sorted and contains the original first j−1 elements. Init: j=2, one element sorted. Maintenance: inserting A[j] keeps it sorted. Termination: j=n+1, whole array sorted.
keyPoints: Three steps: initialisation, maintenance, termination.
Similar to mathematical induction.
Partial correctness: correct if it terminates; total correctness: also terminates.
Invariant should be strong enough to imply the postcondition at termination.
Used for sorting, searching, summing loops.
Correctness is different from efficiency.
ifYouKnow: State and prove a loop invariant.
commonMistakes: Proving only that the invariant holds initially.
Choosing a trivial invariant that doesn't imply the result.

examQuestions.question: Prove correctness of finding the maximum using a loop invariant.
examQuestions.answer: Invariant: max = largest of A[1..i−1]; init i=2; maintenance by compare; termination i=n+1 ⇒ max of all.

examQuestions.question: What are the three properties of a loop invariant?
examQuestions.answer: Initialisation, maintenance, termination.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is NOT a loop-invariant step?
A loop invariant is true before each iteration.
Invariant of insertion sort at iteration j?
Loop never ends but invariant holds. Correctness type lost?
Partial vs total correctness.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Partial: correct if it halts; total: halts and is correct.

daa-c1-t11.quickRevision: Loop invariant: Initialisation + Maintenance + Termination ⇒ correctness (like induction).
algorithmSteps: 1. State the invariant.
2. Show it holds before the first iteration.
3. Assume it holds before iteration k; show it holds before k+1.
4. At loop exit use invariant + exit condition to prove the result.
daa-c1-t11.workedExample: Max(A): invariant 'max = largest of A[1..i−1]'. Init: i=2, max=A[1] ✓. Maintenance: compare A[i] with max ✓. Termination: i=n+1 ⇒ max = largest of A[1..n].

daa-c1-t12.title: Recurrences
daa-c1-t12.definition: A recurrence relation expresses the running time of a recursive algorithm in terms of its running time on smaller inputs, solved by substitution, recursion tree or master method.
daa-c1-t12.simpleExplanation: Recursive algorithm ka time T(n) khud T(chhota n) se likhte hain, jaise T(n)=2T(n/2)+n. Isko solve karne ke 3 tareeke: substitution, recursion tree, master method.
daa-c1-t12.realLifeAnalogy: A pizza chain: cost of serving n customers = cost of serving two halves + time to split and merge.
daa-c1-t12.example: Merge sort: T(n)=2T(n/2)+n. Recursion tree: each level costs n and there are log n levels ⇒ Θ(n log n). Master: a=2,b=2,f=n=n^{log₂2} ⇒ case 2 ⇒ Θ(n log n).
keyPoints: Substitution: guess the solution and prove by induction.
Recursion tree: expand levels, sum cost per level, add all levels.
Master theorem for T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n), a≥1, b>1: compare f(n) with n^{log_b a}.
Case 1: f=O(n^{log_b a−ε}) ⇒ Θ(n^{log_b a}).
Case 2: f=Θ(n^{log_b a}) ⇒ Θ(n^{log_b a} log n).
Case 3: f=Ω(n^{log_b a+ε}) and regularity ⇒ Θ(f(n)).
Master theorem does not apply to every recurrence.
ifYouKnow: Solve recurrences by all three methods.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the regularity condition in case 3.
Misreading log_b a (e.g. log₂4 = 2).

examQuestions.question: Solve T(n)=4T(n/2)+n.
examQuestions.answer: a=4,b=2: n^{log₂4}=n²; f=n=O(n^{2−ε}) ⇒ Θ(n²).

examQuestions.question: Solve T(n)=3T(n/2)+n².
examQuestions.answer: n^{1.58}; f=n² larger ⇒ case 3 ⇒ Θ(n²).

examQuestions.question: Explain substitution method for T(n)=2T(n/2)+n.
examQuestions.answer: Guess T(n)≤c n log n; T(n) ≤ 2c(n/2)log(n/2)+n = c n log n − c n + n ≤ c n log n for c ≥ 1.

knowledgeCheck.question: Master theorem needs a ≥ 1 and b > 1.
Recursion tree levels for n/2 splitting?
Substitution vs recursion tree.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Substitution proves a guess by induction; tree helps find the guess by summing level costs.

daa-c1-t12.quickRevision: Recurrence T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n): compare f with n^{log_b a} → Θ(n^{log_b a}), Θ(n^{log_b a} log n) or Θ(f).
algorithmSteps: Master: 1. Identify a, b, f(n).
2. Compute n^{log_b a}.
3. Compare f(n) with it → choose case 1/2/3.
4. Write Θ result (check regularity for case 3).
daa-c1-t12.workedExample: T(n)=2T(n/2)+n: tree levels cost n each, log₂ n+1 levels ⇒ n log n. Master case 2 agrees.

daa-c1-t13.title: Bubble Sort
daa-c1-t13.definition: Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent elements and swaps them if they are in the wrong order, so the largest element 'bubbles' to the end in each pass.
daa-c1-t13.simpleExplanation: Bubble sort adjacent elements ko compare karke swap karta hai. Har pass me sabse bada element end me pahunch jata hai, jaise paani me bubble upar aata hai.
daa-c1-t13.realLifeAnalogy: Bubbles rising in a glass: the biggest bubble reaches the top first.
keyPoints: Compares adjacent pairs; n−1 passes at most.
After pass i the i largest elements are in place.
Number of comparisons n(n−1)/2.
Optimised version stops when a pass has no swap.
Stable and in-place.
Simple but inefficient for large n.
commonMistakes: Thinking bubble sort is always Θ(n²) — optimised best case is Θ(n).
Forgetting n−1−i limit in the inner loop.

examQuestions.question: Sort [5,1,4,2,8] with bubble sort, show passes.
examQuestions.answer: As in example → [1,2,4,5,8].

examQuestions.question: Write algorithm and complexity of bubble sort.
examQuestions.answer: Pseudocode; best O(n) with flag, worst/avg O(n²), space O(1).

examQuestions.question: Is bubble sort stable?
examQuestions.answer: Yes (equal elements are not swapped).

knowledgeCheck.question: Bubble vs selection swaps.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Bubble may do many swaps; selection does at most n−1.

daa-c1-t13.quickRevision: Bubble: swap adjacent out-of-order pairs; n(n−1)/2 comparisons; best O(n) (flag), avg/worst O(n²); stable, in-place.
daa-c1-t13.problemStatement: Sort array A[1..n] in ascending order.
algorithmSteps: 1. For i = 1 to n−1: set swapped=false.
2. For j = 1 to n−i: if A[j] > A[j+1] swap and set swapped=true.
3. If no swap in a pass, stop.
daa-c1-t13.pseudocode:
BubbleSort(A, n)
  for i ← 1 to n−1 do
    swapped ← false
    for j ← 1 to n−i do
      if A[j] > A[j+1] then
        swap A[j], A[j+1]; swapped ← true
    if not swapped then break
daa-c1-t13.timeComplexity: Best O(n), average O(n²), worst O(n²)

daa-c1-t14.title: Selection Sort
daa-c1-t14.definition: Selection sort repeatedly selects the minimum element from the unsorted part and places it at the beginning of the sorted part.
daa-c1-t14.simpleExplanation: Selection sort har baar unsorted part me se sabse chhota element dhundh ke sahi position par swap karta hai. Swaps kam hote hain par comparisons fixed.
daa-c1-t14.realLifeAnalogy: Picking the shortest student in the line and moving him to the front, then repeating for the rest.
keyPoints: Finds min in each pass: n−1 passes.
Always n(n−1)/2 comparisons.
At most n−1 swaps.
Not stable (swap can reorder equals).
In-place, O(1) space.
Same time in best, average and worst case.
commonMistakes: Thinking best case is O(n); it is always Θ(n²).
Assuming it is stable.

examQuestions.question: Why is selection sort not stable?
examQuestions.answer: Long-distance swaps can move equal elements past each other.

knowledgeCheck.question: Selection vs bubble.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Selection fewer swaps; both Θ(n²) comparisons in general.

daa-c1-t14.quickRevision: Selection: pick min each pass; n(n−1)/2 comparisons always; ≤ n−1 swaps; not stable; in-place.
daa-c1-t14.approach: Select the minimum of the unsorted part and swap it into place.
algorithmSteps: 1. For i = 1 to n−1: min = i.
2. For j = i+1 to n: if A[j] < A[min] then min = j.
3. Swap A[i] and A[min].
daa-c1-t14.pseudocode:
SelectionSort(A, n)
  for i ← 1 to n−1 do
    min ← i
    for j ← i+1 to n do
      if A[j] < A[min] then min ← j
    swap A[i], A[min]

daa-c1-t15.title: Insertion Sort
daa-c1-t15.definition: Insertion sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by inserting each new element into its correct position among the already sorted elements.
daa-c1-t15.simpleExplanation: Insertion sort taash ke patte sort karne jaisa hai: ek ek card uthake apni sahi jagah par daal do. Almost sorted data par bahut tez.
daa-c1-t15.realLifeAnalogy: Sorting playing cards in your hand: pick the next card and slide it into place among the sorted ones.
keyPoints: Maintains a sorted prefix; inserts key by shifting larger elements.
Best case O(n) (already sorted); worst O(n²) (reverse).
Stable, in-place, online.
Efficient for small or nearly sorted arrays.
Loop invariant: A[1..j−1] sorted.
Used inside hybrid sorts (e.g. Timsort).
commonMistakes: Swapping repeatedly instead of shifting (inefficient).
Claiming O(n log n) average.

examQuestions.question: Bubble vs selection vs insertion.
examQuestions.answer: Table: all O(n²) worst; insertion best O(n), stable; selection fewest swaps.

examQuestions.question: When is insertion sort best?
examQuestions.answer: Small or nearly sorted input.

daa-c1-t15.quickRevision: Insertion: insert each key into sorted prefix; best O(n), worst/avg O(n²); stable, in-place, online.
daa-c1-t15.approach: Insert A[j] into the sorted prefix A[1..j−1].
algorithmSteps: 1. For j = 2 to n: key = A[j]; i = j−1.
2. While i>0 and A[i] > key: A[i+1] = A[i]; i = i−1.
daa-c1-t15.pseudocode:
InsertionSort(A, n)
  for j ← 2 to n do
    key ← A[j]; i ← j−1
    while i > 0 and A[i] > key do
      A[i+1] ← A[i]; i ← i−1
    A[i+1] ← key
daa-c1-t15.timeComplexity: Best O(n), average O(n²), worst O(n²)

daa-c2-t01.title: Structure of Divide-and-Conquer Algorithms
daa-c2-t01.definition: Divide and conquer solves a problem by dividing it into smaller sub-problems of the same type, solving them recursively and combining their solutions.
daa-c2-t01.simpleExplanation: D&C me problem ko chhote hisso me todo (divide), har hissa solve karo (conquer), phir answers jodo (combine). Merge sort aur quick sort isi tarah kaam karte hain.
daa-c2-t01.realLifeAnalogy: Grading 1000 answer sheets: split among 10 teachers, each grades their share, then the head combines the results.
daa-c2-t01.example: Merge sort: divide array in two halves, sort each recursively, merge the sorted halves. T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n).
keyPoints: Three steps: Divide, Conquer, Combine.
Sub-problems are independent and of the same type.
Base case stops the recursion.
Recurrence: T(n)=aT(n/b)+D(n)+C(n).
Solved with recursion tree/master theorem.
Examples: binary search, merge sort, quick sort, Strassen, max-min.
commonMistakes: Using D&C when sub-problems overlap heavily (DP is better).
Forgetting the base case.

examQuestions.question: Explain the structure of divide-and-conquer algorithms.
examQuestions.answer: Divide, conquer, combine with recurrence and examples.

examQuestions.question: D&C vs DP.
examQuestions.answer: D&C: independent sub-problems; DP: overlapping sub-problems reused.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which is not a D&C step?
Combine step cost in merge sort vs quick sort.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Merge sort: merge costs Θ(n); quick sort: combine is trivial, partition costs Θ(n).

daa-c2-t01.problemStatement: Solve a size-n problem by solving smaller instances.
daa-c2-t01.approach: Split into independent sub-problems, recurse, merge answers.
algorithmSteps: 1. If n is small, solve directly (base case).
2. Divide the problem into a sub-problems of size n/b.
3. Recursively solve each.
4. Combine the sub-solutions.

daa-c2-t02.title: Binary Search
daa-c2-t02.definition: Binary search finds a key in a sorted array by repeatedly comparing it with the middle element and discarding half of the array.
daa-c2-t02.simpleExplanation: Sorted array me beech wala element dekho. Key chhota hai to left half, bada hai to right half. Har step me aadha array hat jata hai, isliye bahut tez.
daa-c2-t02.realLifeAnalogy: Finding a word in a dictionary: open the middle, decide left or right, repeat.
keyPoints: Requires a sorted array.
Each step halves the search space.
Recurrence T(n)=T(n/2)+1 ⇒ O(log n).
Best case O(1); worst O(log n).
Iterative version uses O(1) space; recursive O(log n).
Compute mid as low+(high−low)/2 to avoid overflow.
ifYouKnow: Explain why sorted input is needed.
commonMistakes: Applying it on unsorted data.
Off-by-one errors in low/high updates.

examQuestions.question: Search 23 in the sorted array above.
examQuestions.answer: Index 5 after 3 comparisons.

examQuestions.question: Write algorithm and analyse complexity.
examQuestions.answer: Pseudocode; T(n)=T(n/2)+1 ⇒ Θ(log n).

examQuestions.question: Why log n?
examQuestions.answer: Each comparison halves the remaining elements.

knowledgeCheck.question: Binary search works on unsorted arrays.
Linear vs binary search.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Linear works unsorted, O(n); binary needs sorted, O(log n).

daa-c2-t02.quickRevision: Binary search: sorted array, halve each step; T(n)=T(n/2)+1 ⇒ O(log n); best O(1); iterative space O(1).
daa-c2-t02.problemStatement: Given sorted A[1..n] and key, find its index.
daa-c2-t02.approach: Compare with middle and discard half.
algorithmSteps: 1. low=1, high=n.
2. While low ≤ high: mid=⌊(low+high)/2⌋.
3. If A[mid]=key return mid; if key < A[mid] high=mid−1; else low=mid+1.
4. Return not found.
daa-c2-t02.pseudocode:
BinarySearch(A, n, key)
  low ← 1; high ← n
  while low ≤ high do
    mid ← ⌊(low+high)/2⌋
    if A[mid] = key then return mid
    else if key < A[mid] then high ← mid−1
    else low ← mid+1
  return −1

daa-c2-t03.title: Quick Sort
daa-c2-t03.definition: Quick sort picks a pivot, partitions the array so smaller elements go left and larger go right, then sorts the two parts recursively.
daa-c2-t03.simpleExplanation: Quick sort me ek pivot chunte hain; pivot se chhote left, bade right (partition). Phir dono hisson ko recursively sort karte hain. Average me bahut tez.
daa-c2-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Sorting students by height: pick one student as reference, put shorter ones on the left and taller on the right, repeat inside each group.
daa-c2-t03.example: [10,80,30,90,40,50,70], pivot=70 (Lomuto). After partition: [10,30,40,50,70,90,80] with pivot at index 4 (0-based). Then sort [10,30,40,50] and [90,80].
keyPoints: Divide: partition around pivot; conquer: recurse; combine: nothing.
Best/average Θ(n log n); worst Θ(n²) (already sorted with bad pivot).
In-place; space O(log n) recursion stack average.
Not stable.
Pivot choice: last, first, random, median-of-three.
Randomised pivot makes worst case unlikely.
commonMistakes: Believing worst case is rare for any pivot rule (it occurs for sorted input with first/last pivot).
Partition index off-by-one.

examQuestions.question: Explain quick sort with complexity.
examQuestions.answer: Partition + recursion; best/avg n log n; worst n².

examQuestions.question: When does quick sort degrade to O(n²)?
examQuestions.answer: When partitions are maximally unbalanced, e.g. sorted input with first/last pivot.

knowledgeCheck.question: Sorted array with last-element pivot. Complexity?
Quick sort vs merge sort space.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Quick: O(log n) in-place; merge: O(n) extra.

daa-c2-t03.quickRevision: Quick sort: partition around pivot; avg/best n log n, worst n²; in-place, not stable; random pivot.
daa-c2-t03.approach: Partition around a pivot then sort both sides.
algorithmSteps: 1. If p<r: q = Partition(A,p,r).
2. QuickSort(A,p,q−1).
3. QuickSort(A,q+1,r).
Partition (Lomuto): pivot=A[r]; i=p−1; for j=p..r−1: if A[j] ≤ pivot: i++, swap A[i],A[j]; finally swap A[i+1],A[r]; return i+1.
daa-c2-t03.pseudocode:
QuickSort(A,p,r)
  if p < r then
    q ← Partition(A,p,r)
    QuickSort(A,p,q−1); QuickSort(A,q+1,r)
Partition(A,p,r)
  x ← A[r]; i ← p−1
  for j ← p to r−1 do
    if A[j] ≤ x then i ← i+1; swap A[i],A[j]
  swap A[i+1],A[r]
  return i+1
daa-c2-t03.timeComplexity: Best/average Θ(n log n), worst Θ(n²)
daa-c2-t03.spaceComplexity: O(log n) average, O(n) worst stack

daa-c2-t04.title: Merge Sort
daa-c2-t04.definition: Merge sort divides the array into two halves, sorts each recursively and merges the two sorted halves into one sorted array.
daa-c2-t04.simpleExplanation: Merge sort array ko beech se todta hai, dono halves sort karta hai aur phir do sorted halves ko merge karta hai. Time hamesha n log n.
daa-c2-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Two sorted piles of cards are merged by repeatedly taking the smaller top card.
keyPoints: Divide into halves, recursive sort, merge in Θ(n).
T(n)=2T(n/2)+Θ(n) ⇒ Θ(n log n) in all cases.
Needs O(n) auxiliary space.
Stable.
Not in-place for arrays; good for linked lists and external sorting.
Optimal for comparison sorting.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the auxiliary array cost.
Thinking best case is faster than worst (it is not).

examQuestions.question: Write merge sort and derive its complexity.
examQuestions.answer: Pseudocode; T(n)=2T(n/2)+n ⇒ n log n.

examQuestions.question: Is merge sort stable?
examQuestions.answer: Yes, if the merge takes from the left half when equal.

knowledgeCheck.question: Merge sort worst case is O(n log n).
Merge vs insertion sort.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Merge n log n always; insertion n² worst but n best.

daa-c2-t04.quickRevision: Merge sort: split, sort halves, merge Θ(n); T=2T(n/2)+n ⇒ Θ(n log n) all cases; O(n) space; stable.
daa-c2-t04.approach: Divide into halves, sort recursively, merge.
algorithmSteps: 1. If n ≤ 1 return.
2. mid=⌊(p+r)/2⌋; MergeSort left; MergeSort right.
3. Merge(A,p,mid,r): copy halves, take smaller front element repeatedly.
daa-c2-t04.pseudocode:
MergeSort(A,p,r)
  if p < r then
    q ← ⌊(p+r)/2⌋
    MergeSort(A,p,q); MergeSort(A,q+1,r)
    Merge(A,p,q,r)

daa-c2-t05.title: Strassen Multiplication
daa-c2-t05.definition: Strassen's algorithm multiplies two n×n matrices with seven recursive sub-multiplications instead of eight, giving Θ(n^{log₂7}) ≈ Θ(n^{2.81}).
daa-c2-t05.simpleExplanation: Normal matrix multiplication n³ hai. Strassen 2×2 block ke liye 8 ke jagah 7 multiplications use karta hai, isliye bade matrices par fast.
daa-c2-t05.realLifeAnalogy: Finding a shortcut that saves one of the eight expensive trips each time you cross a bridge.
keyPoints: Classical D&C: 8 multiplications ⇒ T=8T(n/2)+n² ⇒ Θ(n³).
Strassen: 7 multiplications ⇒ T=7T(n/2)+Θ(n²) ⇒ Θ(n^{log₂7}).
More additions/subtractions (18) but fewer multiplications.
Requires n to be a power of 2 (pad with zeros).
Higher constants and numerical stability issues; useful for large n.
Idea: algebraic identity reduces the multiplication count.
commonMistakes: Believing Strassen is always faster in practice (constants).
Forgetting padding to a power of two.

knowledgeCheck.question: Classical D&C vs Strassen.
knowledgeCheck.answer: 8 vs 7 recursive multiplications; n³ vs n^2.81.

daa-c2-t05.quickRevision: Strassen: 7 mults instead of 8; T=7T(n/2)+n² ⇒ Θ(n^{2.81}); formulas M1–M7.
daa-c2-t05.approach: Use 7 clever products of sums/differences of sub-blocks.
algorithmSteps: 1. Split A,B,C into n/2×n/2 blocks.
daa-c2-t05.workedExample: A=[[1,2],[3,4]], B=[[5,6],[7,8]] ⇒ C=[[19,22],[43,50]] (checked against normal multiplication).

daa-c2-t06.title: Max-Min Problem
daa-c2-t06.definition: The Max-Min problem finds the maximum and minimum of n elements; divide and conquer solves it using about 3n/2 − 2 comparisons instead of 2(n−1).
daa-c2-t06.simpleExplanation: Max aur min dono nikalne hain. Normal tareeke se 2(n−1) comparisons lagte hain. D&C me array ko do hisson me baant ke har hisse ke max-min nikalte hain, comparisons ~3n/2 − 2.
daa-c2-t06.realLifeAnalogy: Finding the tallest and shortest in a class by splitting into groups, finding each group's tallest and shortest, then comparing group winners.
keyPoints: Naive: 2(n−1) comparisons.
D&C recurrence: T(n)=2T(n/2)+2, T(2)=1, T(1)=0.
Solution: T(n)=3n/2 − 2 (n power of 2).
Time Θ(n); this is optimal in the number of comparisons.
Base cases: one element, or two elements (1 comparison).
Combine step: 2 comparisons.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the two comparisons in combine.
Applying formula when n is not a power of 2 without adjusting.

examQuestions.question: Find max/min of [3,9,1,7] by D&C; count comparisons.
examQuestions.answer: max 9, min 1; 4 comparisons.

knowledgeCheck.question: Time complexity naive vs D&C.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Both Θ(n); D&C uses fewer comparisons.

daa-c2-t06.problemStatement: Find max and min of A[1..n].
daa-c2-t06.approach: Split, find max/min in halves, combine with 2 comparisons.
algorithmSteps: 1. If n=1: max=min=A[i]. If n=2: one comparison.
2. Else split; solve both halves.
3. max=larger of the two maxes; min=smaller of the two mins.
daa-c2-t06.pseudocode:
MaxMin(i,j,max,min)
  if i=j then max←min←A[i]
  else if j=i+1 then
    if A[i]<A[j] then max←A[j]; min←A[i] else max←A[i]; min←A[j]
  else
    mid←⌊(i+j)/2⌋
    MaxMin(i,mid,max1,min1); MaxMin(mid+1,j,max2,min2)
    max←MAX(max1,max2); min←MIN(min1,min2)
daa-c2-t06.workedExample: [3,9,1,7]: halves → (9,3) and (7,1) → max 9, min 1; total 4 comparisons.

daa-c3-t01.title: Introduction to Greedy Algorithms
daa-c3-t01.definition: A greedy algorithm builds a solution step by step, always choosing the option that looks best at the moment, hoping to reach a global optimum.
daa-c3-t01.simpleExplanation: Greedy me har step par sabse achha lagne wala choice le lete hain aur use badalte nahi. Kuch problems me ye optimal deta hai, kuch me nahi.
daa-c3-t01.realLifeAnalogy: Giving change by always handing the biggest coin that fits.
daa-c3-t01.example: Coins {25,10,5,1}, amount 41 → 25+10+5+1 (4 coins) optimal. But coins {1,3,4}, amount 6: greedy 4+1+1 (3 coins) while optimal 3+3 (2 coins) — greedy fails.
keyPoints: Make locally optimal choice at each step; never backtrack.
Works if greedy-choice property and optimal substructure hold.
Typically sort + select; fast and simple.
Examples: Kruskal, Prim, Dijkstra, Huffman, activity selection, fractional knapsack.
Not guaranteed optimal for all problems (0/1 knapsack, arbitrary coins).
Proof via exchange argument.
commonMistakes: Assuming greedy is always optimal.
Not proving the greedy-choice property.

examQuestions.question: Explain greedy strategy with a counterexample.
examQuestions.answer: Local best choices; coin change {1,3,4} for 6.

examQuestions.question: Greedy vs DP.
examQuestions.answer: Greedy makes one irrevocable choice; DP evaluates all sub-problems.

knowledgeCheck.question: Greedy is NOT guaranteed optimal for:
Choosing the earliest finishing activity first is…
Greedy vs brute force.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Greedy is fast but may be suboptimal; brute force is exhaustive.

daa-c3-t01.quickRevision: Greedy: best local choice, no backtracking; needs greedy-choice + optimal substructure; fails for 0/1 knapsack.
daa-c3-t01.problemStatement: Optimise an objective by sequential choices.
daa-c3-t01.approach: Pick the locally best feasible candidate each step.
algorithmSteps: 1. Initialise solution as empty.
2. Select the best candidate by the greedy rule.
3. If feasible add it; else discard.
4. Repeat until a complete solution.
daa-c3-t01.timeComplexity: Usually O(n log n) due to sorting

daa-c3-t02.title: Elements of Greedy Strategy
daa-c3-t02.definition: The elements of a greedy strategy are a candidate set, selection function, feasibility function, objective function and solution function, justified by the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure.
daa-c3-t02.simpleExplanation: Greedy algorithm ke 5 hisse: candidates ka set, selection function (best kaun), feasibility (add kar sakte hain?), objective (kya maximize/minimize), solution (complete hua?). Sahi hone ke liye greedy-choice property aur optimal substructure chahiye.
daa-c3-t02.realLifeAnalogy: Packing a bag: items to choose from (candidates), your preference (selection), weight limit (feasibility), total value (objective), bag full (solution).
daa-c3-t02.example: Activity selection: candidates = activities; selection = earliest finish time; feasibility = no overlap with chosen; objective = maximise count; solution = no more feasible activity.
keyPoints: Candidate set, selection function, feasibility function, objective function, solution function.
Greedy-choice property: a locally optimal choice is part of some globally optimal solution.
Optimal substructure: optimal solution contains optimal solutions of sub-problems.
Proof technique: exchange argument.
Matroid structure guarantees greedy optimality for certain problems.
Without these properties greedy can fail.
commonMistakes: Confusing greedy-choice property with optimal substructure.
Skipping the proof of correctness.

examQuestions.question: Explain elements of greedy strategy.
examQuestions.answer: Five functions + two properties with activity selection mapping.

examQuestions.question: What is the greedy-choice property?
examQuestions.answer: A globally optimal solution can be built from locally optimal choices.

knowledgeCheck.question: Checks whether a candidate can be added:
Define optimal substructure.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Optimal solution contains optimal solutions to sub-problems.

knowledgeCheck.question: Selection vs feasibility function.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Selection chooses the best candidate; feasibility checks if it keeps a valid solution.

daa-c3-t02.quickRevision: Greedy elements: candidates, selection, feasibility, objective, solution; properties: greedy-choice + optimal substructure.

daa-c3-t03.title: Minimum Spanning Tree
daa-c3-t03.definition: A minimum spanning tree (MST) of a connected weighted graph is a spanning tree with the least total edge weight; Kruskal's and Prim's greedy algorithms find it.
daa-c3-t03.simpleExplanation: MST graph ke saare vertices ko sabse kam total weight me jodta hai bina cycle ke. Kruskal edges ko sort karke cycle na banne wali edges leta hai; Prim ek vertex se shuru karke sabse sasti edge se tree badhata hai.
daa-c3-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Laying the cheapest cable to connect all villages without wasting wire.
daa-c3-t03.example: Edges: AB1, BC2, AC3, BD4, CD5, CE6, DE7. Kruskal: AB1 ✓, BC2 ✓, AC3 ✗(cycle), BD4 ✓, CD5 ✗, CE6 ✓ → MST weight 1+2+4+6=13. Prim from A gives the same weight 13.
keyPoints: Spanning tree has V−1 edges, no cycles.
Cut property: the lightest edge crossing a cut is in some MST.
Kruskal: sort edges; add if no cycle (union-find). Time O(E log E).
Prim: grow tree from a start vertex using min edge to a new vertex. O(V²) array, O(E log V) heap.
Kruskal is edge-based; Prim vertex-based.
MST is not necessarily unique when weights tie.
commonMistakes: Adding edges that form a cycle.
Using Prim's with disconnected graph without care.

examQuestions.question: Find MST of the given graph by Kruskal.
examQuestions.answer: Edges AB, BC, BD, CE; weight 13.

examQuestions.question: Kruskal vs Prim.
examQuestions.answer: Kruskal: global sorted edges, union-find, good for sparse; Prim: grows one tree, good for dense.

examQuestions.question: How many edges in an MST of V vertices?

daa-c3-t03.quickRevision: MST: V−1 edges, min weight; Kruskal (sort edges + union-find, O(E log E)); Prim (grow tree, O(E log V)).
daa-c3-t03.problemStatement: Connect all vertices of a weighted graph with minimum total weight.
daa-c3-t03.approach: Greedily add the cheapest safe edge (cut property).
algorithmSteps: Kruskal: 1. Sort edges by weight.
2. For each edge (u,v): if Find(u)≠Find(v) add edge and Union(u,v).
3. Stop at V−1 edges.
Prim: 1. Pick start s, key[s]=0.
2. Repeatedly add the vertex with minimum key (edge to tree).
3. Update keys of its neighbours.
daa-c3-t03.pseudocode:
Kruskal(G)
  A ← ∅; sort edges by weight
  for each edge (u,v) in order do
    if Find(u) ≠ Find(v) then A ← A ∪ {(u,v)}; Union(u,v)
  return A
daa-c3-t03.workedExample: Graph AB1, BC2, AC3, BD4, CD5, CE6, DE7: Kruskal picks AB, BC, BD, CE; total 13.
daa-c3-t03.timeComplexity: Kruskal O(E log E); Prim O(E log V) heap / O(V²) array

daa-c3-t04.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
daa-c3-t04.definition: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source vertex to all other vertices in a graph with non-negative edge weights by greedily settling the nearest unvisited vertex.
daa-c3-t04.simpleExplanation: Dijkstra source se sabhi vertices tak sabse chhota raasta nikalta hai. Har baar sabse kam distance wala vertex finalize karta hai aur uske neighbours ki distance relax karta hai. Negative edges par kaam nahi karta.
daa-c3-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Google Maps finding the fastest route: expand from your location to the nearest places first.
daa-c3-t04.example: Edges: A→B 4, A→C 1, C→B 2, B→D 1, C→D 5. From A: dist A=0, C=1, B=min(4,1+2)=3, D=min(3+1,1+5)=4. Shortest A→D = 4 via A–C–B–D.
keyPoints: Single-source shortest path; weights ≥ 0.
Greedy: pick unvisited vertex with the smallest distance.
Relaxation: if d[u]+w < d[v] update d[v].
O(V²) with array; O((V+E) log V) with min-heap.
Fails with negative edges (use Bellman–Ford).
Path recovered via parent pointers.
ifYouKnow: Explain why not with negative edges.
commonMistakes: Using Dijkstra with negative weights.
Forgetting to update after relaxing.

examQuestions.question: Run Dijkstra on A→B4, A→C1, C→B2, B→D1, C→D5 from A.
Why does Dijkstra fail for negative edges?
examQuestions.answer: A settled vertex's distance may later improve through a negative edge, breaking the greedy assumption.

knowledgeCheck.question: Dijkstra vs Bellman–Ford.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Dijkstra faster, non-negative only; Bellman–Ford handles negative edges.

daa-c3-t04.quickRevision: Dijkstra: single-source, w≥0; pick min-dist vertex, relax; O((V+E)log V); fails with negative edges.
daa-c3-t04.problemStatement: Shortest paths from source s to all vertices.
daa-c3-t04.approach: Repeatedly finalise the closest unvisited vertex and relax its edges.
algorithmSteps: 2. Insert all vertices in a min-priority queue.
3. Extract u with min d[u].
4. For each edge (u,v): if d[u]+w(u,v) < d[v] then d[v]=d[u]+w.
5. Repeat until the queue is empty.
daa-c3-t04.pseudocode:
Dijkstra(G,s)
  for each v: d[v]←∞; d[s]←0
  Q ← all vertices
  while Q not empty do
    u ← ExtractMin(Q)
    for each edge (u,v) do
      if d[u]+w(u,v) < d[v] then d[v] ← d[u]+w(u,v)
daa-c3-t04.workedExample: Start A: relax B=4, C=1. Take C: B=3, D=6. Take B(3): D=4. Take D. Final: A0,C1,B3,D4.
daa-c3-t04.timeComplexity: O(V²) array; O((V+E) log V) heap

daa-c3-t05.title: Knapsack Problem
daa-c3-t05.definition: The (fractional) knapsack problem selects items, possibly fractions of them, to maximise total value within a weight capacity; the greedy choice by value-to-weight ratio is optimal.
daa-c3-t05.simpleExplanation: Bag ki capacity limited hai, items ka value aur weight hai. Fractional knapsack me item ka hissa le sakte ho, isliye value/weight ratio ke hisaab se sabse zyada ratio wala pehle lo — greedy optimal.
daa-c3-t05.realLifeAnalogy: Filling a jar with gold dust, silver and copper: take the most valuable per gram first.
keyPoints: Fractional: items divisible ⇒ greedy by v/w ratio is optimal.
0/1 knapsack: items indivisible ⇒ greedy may fail (use DP).
Steps: compute ratios, sort descending, fill.
Time O(n log n) due to sorting.
Example 0/1 optimum for above is 220 (items 2+3), greedy 0/1 would give 160.
Takes whole items first and a fraction of the last.
commonMistakes: Applying ratio-greedy to 0/1 and claiming optimality.
Forgetting to take the fractional part.

examQuestions.question: Fractional vs 0/1 knapsack.
examQuestions.answer: Fractional: greedy optimal, O(n log n); 0/1: needs DP, O(nW).

daa-c3-t05.quickRevision: Fractional knapsack: sort by v/w desc, take whole items then a fraction; O(n log n); example 240 (0/1 optimum 220).
daa-c3-t05.problemStatement: Maximise total value of items in capacity W; fractions allowed.
daa-c3-t05.approach: Take items in decreasing value/weight order.
algorithmSteps: 1. Compute v_i/w_i for all items.
2. Sort descending by ratio.
3. For each item: if it fits take it all, else take the fitting fraction and stop.
daa-c3-t05.pseudocode:
FractionalKnapsack(v,w,W,n)
  sort items by v[i]/w[i] descending
  total ← 0
  for i ← 1 to n do
    if w[i] ≤ W then total += v[i]; W −= w[i]
    else total += v[i]·(W/w[i]); break
  return total

daa-c3-t06.title: Activity Selection Problem
daa-c3-t06.definition: The activity selection problem chooses the maximum number of mutually compatible (non-overlapping) activities; greedily selecting the earliest finishing activity is optimal.
daa-c3-t06.simpleExplanation: Ek room me zyada se zyada activities fit karni hain jo overlap na karein. Activities ko finish time ke hisaab se sort karo, sabse jaldi khatam hone wali lo, phir agli jo uske baad start ho.
daa-c3-t06.realLifeAnalogy: Booking the most meetings in one room: always pick the meeting that ends earliest.
keyPoints: Sort by finish time.
Pick first; then each next with start ≥ last finish.
Greedy-choice property proven by exchange argument.
Time O(n log n) (sorting), O(n) after.
Maximises count, not total time.
Used in scheduling.
commonMistakes: Sorting by start time or duration (not optimal).
Allowing start < last finish.

examQuestions.question: Select max activities from the given list.
Why earliest finish time?
examQuestions.answer: It leaves the most room for remaining activities.

knowledgeCheck.question: Earliest start vs earliest finish.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Earliest start can pick a long activity blocking others; earliest finish is optimal.

daa-c3-t06.quickRevision: Activity selection: sort by finish, take compatible (start ≥ last finish); O(n log n).
daa-c3-t06.problemStatement: Pick the maximum number of non-overlapping activities.
daa-c3-t06.approach: Always choose the activity that finishes earliest.
algorithmSteps: 1. Sort by finish time.
2. Select the first activity.
3. For each next activity: if start ≥ finish of last selected, select it.
daa-c3-t06.pseudocode:
ActivitySelection(s,f,n)
  sort by f
  A ← {1}; last ← 1
  for i ← 2 to n do
    if s[i] ≥ f[last] then A ← A ∪ {i}; last ← i
  return A

daa-c3-t07.title: Huffman Codes
daa-c3-t07.definition: Huffman coding is a greedy algorithm that builds an optimal prefix-free binary code, giving shorter codes to more frequent characters to compress data.
daa-c3-t07.simpleExplanation: Huffman me jo character zyada aata hai usko chhota code, kam aane wale ko lamba code dete hain. Prefix-free hota hai, isliye decode me confusion nahi. Greedy tarike se do sabse kam frequency wale nodes ko merge karte jaate hain.
daa-c3-t07.realLifeAnalogy: Morse code idea: frequent letters like E get short signals, rare ones get long.
keyPoints: Prefix code: no code is a prefix of another.
Greedy: repeatedly merge the two lowest-frequency nodes using a min-heap.
Left edge = 0, right edge = 1.
Optimal among prefix codes.
Time O(n log n) with heap.
Used in compression (e.g. JPEG, ZIP stages).
commonMistakes: Not keeping the code prefix-free.
Mis-merging: always pick the two smallest.

examQuestions.question: What is a prefix code?
examQuestions.answer: A code in which no codeword is a prefix of another.

knowledgeCheck.question: Fixed vs Huffman coding.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Fixed uses equal length codes; Huffman uses variable length by frequency (fewer bits overall).

daa-c3-t07.quickRevision: Huffman: merge two smallest freq repeatedly (min-heap); prefix-free; O(n log n); example total 224 bits.
daa-c3-t07.problemStatement: Assign binary codes to characters minimising total encoded length.
daa-c3-t07.approach: Greedily merge the two least frequent nodes.
algorithmSteps: 1. Create a leaf per character; build a min-heap by frequency.
2. Repeat n−1 times: extract two minimum nodes; create parent with sum frequency; insert.
3. Assign 0 to left, 1 to right; read codes from root to leaves.
daa-c3-t07.pseudocode:
Huffman(C)
  n ← |C|; Q ← C (min-heap by freq)
  for i ← 1 to n−1 do
    z ← new node
    z.left ← ExtractMin(Q); z.right ← ExtractMin(Q)
    z.freq ← z.left.freq + z.right.freq
    Insert(Q, z)
  return ExtractMin(Q)

daa-c4-t01.title: Principle of Optimality
daa-c4-t01.definition: The principle of optimality states that an optimal solution to a problem contains optimal solutions to its sub-problems; dynamic programming exploits this together with overlapping sub-problems.
daa-c4-t01.simpleExplanation: Dynamic programming me bade problem ka optimal answer chhote problems ke optimal answers se banta hai. Sub-problems repeat hote hain, isliye unka answer store karke dobara compute nahi karte.
daa-c4-t01.realLifeAnalogy: Planning the cheapest route Delhi→Mumbai via Jaipur: the Jaipur→Mumbai part must itself be the cheapest from Jaipur.
daa-c4-t01.example: Fibonacci: naive recursion recomputes F(k) many times (O(2ⁿ)). DP stores F(0..n) in a table: F(n)=F(n−1)+F(n−2) computed once each ⇒ O(n).
keyPoints: Needs optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems.
Top-down (memoization) vs bottom-up (tabulation).
Steps: define sub-problem, recurrence, base case, fill table, reconstruct answer.
Trades memory for time.
Examples: 0/1 knapsack, LCS, chain matrix, Floyd–Warshall, making change.
Different from greedy: tries all sub-problem options.
commonMistakes: Using DP without overlapping sub-problems (no benefit).
Assuming greedy and DP are the same.

examQuestions.question: Explain principle of optimality with an example.
examQuestions.answer: Optimal substructure; shortest path via an intermediate vertex.

examQuestions.question: Memoization vs tabulation.
examQuestions.answer: Top-down recursion with cache vs bottom-up table filling.

knowledgeCheck.question: DP vs D&C.
knowledgeCheck.answer: DP reuses overlapping sub-problems; D&C sub-problems are independent.

daa-c4-t01.quickRevision: Optimality: optimal solution built from optimal sub-solutions; DP = optimal substructure + overlapping sub-problems; memoize or tabulate.
daa-c4-t01.problemStatement: Solve problems with optimal substructure and repeating sub-problems efficiently.
daa-c4-t01.approach: Store each sub-problem's answer once and reuse it.
algorithmSteps: 1. Characterise the optimal structure.
2. Write a recurrence with base cases.
3. Fill the table bottom-up (or memoise top-down).
4. Reconstruct the solution from the table.
daa-c4-t01.pseudocode:
Fib(n)
  F[0]←0; F[1]←1
  for i ← 2 to n do F[i] ← F[i−1] + F[i−2]
  return F[n]
daa-c4-t01.workedExample: F: 0,1,1,2,3,5,8 … each computed once; naive recursion for F(5) recomputes F(2) three times.

daa-c4-t02.title: 0/1 Knapsack Problem
daa-c4-t02.definition: The 0/1 knapsack problem chooses a subset of indivisible items maximising total value without exceeding capacity W; it is solved by dynamic programming in O(nW).
daa-c4-t02.simpleExplanation: 0/1 knapsack me item ya to poora lo ya bilkul nahi. Greedy yahan fail ho sakta hai, isliye DP table V[i][w] banate hain: i items aur w capacity me best value.
daa-c4-t02.realLifeAnalogy: Packing a suitcase with fixed-size items: you can't cut a laptop in half.
daa-c4-t02.example: W=7; items (weight,value): (1,1),(3,4),(4,5),(5,7). Final table row 4: [0,1,1,4,5,7,8,9]. Best value 9 using items 2 and 3 (weights 3+4=7).
keyPoints: Recurrence: V[i,w]=V[i−1,w] if wᵢ>w, else max(V[i−1,w], vᵢ+V[i−1,w−wᵢ]).
Time O(nW), space O(nW) (O(W) with 1-D array) — pseudo-polynomial.
Trace back the table to find chosen items.
Greedy by ratio is not optimal here.
NP-hard in general.
commonMistakes: Using greedy ratio for 0/1.
Wrong index when item doesn't fit.

examQuestions.question: Solve W=7 with items (1,1),(3,4),(4,5),(5,7).
examQuestions.answer: Max value 9, items 2 and 3.

examQuestions.question: Write recurrence and complexity.
examQuestions.answer: As above; O(nW).

examQuestions.question: Why is O(nW) pseudo-polynomial?
examQuestions.answer: W is a numeric value, not input length.

knowledgeCheck.question: Greedy ratio is always optimal for 0/1.

daa-c4-t02.quickRevision: 0/1 Knapsack: V[i,w]=max(V[i−1,w], vᵢ+V[i−1,w−wᵢ]); O(nW) time/space; trace back chosen items.
daa-c4-t02.problemStatement: Maximise value of items in capacity W; each item taken whole or not.
daa-c4-t02.approach: Table of best values for first i items and capacity w.
algorithmSteps: 2. For i=1..n, w=1..W: if wᵢ>w V[i][w]=V[i−1][w] else V[i][w]=max(V[i−1][w], vᵢ+V[i−1][w−wᵢ]).
3. Answer V[n][W]; trace back.
daa-c4-t02.pseudocode:
Knapsack(v,w,n,W)
  for i ← 0 to n: V[i][0] ← 0
  for j ← 0 to W: V[0][j] ← 0
  for i ← 1 to n do
    for j ← 1 to W do
      if w[i] > j then V[i][j] ← V[i−1][j]
      else V[i][j] ← max(V[i−1][j], v[i]+V[i−1][j−w[i]])
  return V[n][W]

daa-c4-t03.title: Making Change Problem
daa-c4-t03.definition: The making change problem finds the minimum number of coins needed to form a given amount from given denominations; dynamic programming guarantees the optimum where greedy may fail.
daa-c4-t03.simpleExplanation: Amount N banane ke liye kam se kam coins chahiye. Greedy kabhi galat ho sakta hai, isliye C[j] = min(C[j−coin]+1) wali DP table banate hain.
daa-c4-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Paying exact change at a shop using the fewest coins from a mixed set of denominations.
keyPoints: Recurrence: C[0]=0; C[j]=min over coins d≤j of (C[j−d]+1).
Time O(n·N) for n coins and amount N.
Space O(N).
Greedy works only for canonical coin systems (e.g. 1,5,10,25).
Counting ways variant uses addition instead of min.
Trace back with a 'last coin' array.
commonMistakes: Initialising C[j] to 0 instead of ∞.
Assuming greedy is always valid.

examQuestions.question: Minimum coins for 6 with {1,3,4}.
examQuestions.answer: 2 coins (3+3).

examQuestions.question: Explain DP for making change.
examQuestions.answer: Recurrence, table, complexity.

knowledgeCheck.question: Min-coins vs count-ways.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Min uses min(); count-ways sums combinations.

daa-c4-t03.quickRevision: Making change: C[j]=min(C[j−d]+1); O(nN); greedy fails for {1,3,4}.
daa-c4-t03.problemStatement: Minimise coins to make amount N.
daa-c4-t03.approach: Build answers for amounts 0..N using smaller amounts.
algorithmSteps: 2. For j=1..N: for each coin d≤j: C[j]=min(C[j], C[j−d]+1).
3. Return C[N].
daa-c4-t03.pseudocode:
MakeChange(d,n,N)
  C[0] ← 0
  for j ← 1 to N do
    C[j] ← ∞
    for i ← 1 to n do
      if d[i] ≤ j and C[j−d[i]]+1 < C[j] then C[j] ← C[j−d[i]]+1
  return C[N]

daa-c4-t04.title: Chain Matrix Multiplication
daa-c4-t04.definition: Chain matrix multiplication finds the parenthesisation of a matrix product A₁A₂…Aₙ that minimises the number of scalar multiplications, using dynamic programming.
daa-c4-t04.simpleExplanation: Matrices ko multiply karne ka order alag ho sakta hai aur cost bhi badal jata hai. DP se pata lagate hain kaunsa bracket order sabse kam multiplications deta hai.
daa-c4-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Choosing which pairs of boxes to combine first so total packing effort is least.
keyPoints: Multiplying p×q by q×r costs p·q·r.
m[i,j]=min over k of m[i,k]+m[k+1,j]+p_{i−1}p_k p_j; m[i,i]=0.
Compute by increasing chain length.
Time O(n³), space O(n²).
Number of parenthesisations is a Catalan number (exponential).
Store split points s[i,j] to print the order.
commonMistakes: Forgetting matrix multiplication is associative but cost differs.
Using wrong dimension index p_{i−1}.

examQuestions.question: Dimensions 10×30, 30×5, 5×60: minimum cost and order.
examQuestions.answer: 4500 with (A1A2)A3.

examQuestions.question: Write the recurrence and complexity.
examQuestions.answer: As above; O(n³).

knowledgeCheck.question: Order of parenthesisation changes the result.
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It changes cost, not the result.

knowledgeCheck.question: Brute force vs DP.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Brute force Catalan exponential; DP O(n³).

daa-c4-t04.quickRevision: Chain matrix: m[i,j]=min(m[i,k]+m[k+1,j]+p_{i−1}p_k p_j); O(n³); example 4500 vs 27000.
daa-c4-t04.problemStatement: Minimise scalar multiplications to compute A₁…Aₙ.
daa-c4-t04.approach: Try every split point k and store best costs for sub-chains.
algorithmSteps: 2. For chain length L=2..n, for i, j=i+L−1: m[i,j]=∞.
3. For k=i..j−1: q=m[i,k]+m[k+1,j]+p_{i−1}p_kp_j; keep the minimum and split k.
4. m[1,n] is the answer.
daa-c4-t04.pseudocode:
MatrixChain(p,n)
  for i ← 1 to n: m[i][i] ← 0
  for L ← 2 to n do
    for i ← 1 to n−L+1 do
      j ← i+L−1; m[i][j] ← ∞
      for k ← i to j−1 do
        q ← m[i][k]+m[k+1][j]+p[i−1]·p[k]·p[j]
        if q < m[i][j] then m[i][j] ← q; s[i][j] ← k

daa-c4-t05.title: Longest Common Subsequence
daa-c4-t05.definition: The longest common subsequence (LCS) of two sequences is the longest sequence appearing in both in the same order (not necessarily contiguous).
daa-c4-t05.simpleExplanation: LCS do strings me common letters ka sabse lamba sequence hai jo order me ho par saath-saath hona zaroori nahi. DP table c[i][j] se nikalte hain.
daa-c4-t05.realLifeAnalogy: Finding the longest list of songs that appear in the same order in two playlists, even with other songs between.
daa-c4-t05.example: X=ABCD, Y=ACBD. LCS length 3 (e.g. ABD). Table rows: A:[1,1,1,1], B:[1,1,2,2], C:[1,2,2,2], D:[1,2,2,3].
keyPoints: Recurrence: c[i][j]=c[i−1][j−1]+1 if X[i]=Y[j]; else max(c[i−1][j], c[i][j−1]); c[0][·]=c[·][0]=0.
Time O(mn), space O(mn).
Trace back from c[m][n] to print the subsequence.
Subsequence ≠ substring.
LCS may not be unique.
Used in diff tools, DNA comparison.
commonMistakes: Confusing subsequence with substring.
Wrong tie handling in trace back.

examQuestions.question: LCS length of ABCD and ACBD.
Write algorithm and complexity.
examQuestions.answer: Recurrence; O(mn).

knowledgeCheck.question: LCS vs longest common substring.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Substring must be contiguous; subsequence need not.

daa-c4-t05.quickRevision: LCS: c[i][j]=c[i−1][j−1]+1 if match else max(up,left); O(mn); trace back to read sequence.
daa-c4-t05.problemStatement: Find the longest common subsequence of X[1..m] and Y[1..n].
daa-c4-t05.approach: Table of LCS lengths of prefixes.
algorithmSteps: 2. For i,j: if X[i]=Y[j] c[i][j]=c[i−1][j−1]+1 else c[i][j]=max(c[i−1][j], c[i][j−1]).
3. Trace back from c[m][n].
daa-c4-t05.pseudocode:
LCS(X,Y,m,n)
  for i ← 0 to m: c[i][0] ← 0
  for j ← 0 to n: c[0][j] ← 0
  for i ← 1 to m do
    for j ← 1 to n do
      if X[i]=Y[j] then c[i][j] ← c[i−1][j−1]+1
      else c[i][j] ← max(c[i−1][j], c[i][j−1])
  return c[m][n]
daa-c4-t05.workedExample: X=ABCD, Y=ACBD → last cell c[4][4]=3 → e.g. A,B,D.

daa-c4-t06.title: All Pair Shortest Paths: Warshall's and Floyd's Algorithms
daa-c4-t06.definition: Floyd's algorithm computes shortest distances between all vertex pairs by allowing vertices as intermediates one at a time, and Warshall's algorithm computes reachability (transitive closure) in the same way.
daa-c4-t06.simpleExplanation: Floyd–Warshall har pair (i,j) ka shortest path nikalta hai, ek ek vertex k ko intermediate maan ke: d[i][j]=min(d[i][j], d[i][k]+d[k][j]). Warshall wahi idea reachability (0/1) ke liye.
daa-c4-t06.realLifeAnalogy: Checking whether going via city k shortens every trip between every pair of cities, for each city k in turn.
keyPoints: Warshall: R^(k)[i][j]=R^(k−1)[i][j] OR (R^(k−1)[i][k] AND R^(k−1)[k][j]).
Time Θ(V³), space Θ(V²) (in-place).
Handles negative edges but not negative cycles.
Dynamic programming over intermediate vertices.
Dense graphs: better than running Dijkstra V times with arrays.
commonMistakes: Wrong loop order (k must be the outermost loop).
Using it with negative cycles.

examQuestions.question: Floyd vs Warshall.
examQuestions.answer: Floyd: shortest distances; Warshall: reachability (boolean).

knowledgeCheck.question: d13 after k=2 in the example.
Floyd vs Dijkstra for all pairs.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Floyd Θ(V³) simple; Dijkstra×V is O(V(V+E)logV) for non-negative sparse graphs.

daa-c4-t06.quickRevision: Floyd: d[i][j]=min(d[i][j], d[i][k]+d[k][j]), k outermost, Θ(V³); Warshall: reachability with OR/AND.
daa-c4-t06.problemStatement: Shortest distance between every pair of vertices.
daa-c4-t06.approach: Allow vertices 1..k as intermediates, increasing k.
algorithmSteps: 1. D = weight matrix (∞ if no edge, 0 diagonal).
2. For k=1..n: for i=1..n: for j=1..n: D[i][j]=min(D[i][j], D[i][k]+D[k][j]).
3. D holds all-pairs shortest distances.
daa-c4-t06.pseudocode:
Floyd(W,n)
  D ← W
  for k ← 1 to n do
    for i ← 1 to n do
      for j ← 1 to n do
        D[i][j] ← min(D[i][j], D[i][k]+D[k][j])
  return D

daa-c5-t01.title: An Introduction using Graphs and Games
daa-c5-t01.definition: Many games and puzzles can be modelled as graphs where vertices are game positions and edges are legal moves, so solving the game becomes analysing the graph.
daa-c5-t01.simpleExplanation: Game ko graph samjho: har position ek vertex, har legal move ek edge. Phir graph search se pata chalta hai kaunsi position jeetne wali hai aur kaunsi harne wali.
daa-c5-t01.realLifeAnalogy: A board game map: each square is a position and arrows show where a move can take you.
daa-c5-t01.example: Game: pile of n coins; a move removes 1 or 2; the player who takes the last coin wins. Positions n=0 (player to move has lost), 1 and 2 are winning, 3 is losing, 4 and 5 winning, 6 losing… Losing positions are multiples of 3.
keyPoints: Vertex = position/state; edge = legal move.
Directed graph for games (moves are one-way).
Terminal positions decide win/lose; label backwards.
A position is winning if some move leads to a losing position.
Same modelling for puzzles: 8-puzzle, maze, Nim.
Graph traversal (BFS/DFS) explores the state space.
ifYouKnow: Model a game as a graph.
commonMistakes: Forgetting direction of moves.
Labelling forward instead of from terminal positions backward.

examQuestions.question: Coin game with moves 1 or 2: which n are losing?
examQuestions.answer: Multiples of 3.

examQuestions.question: How are graphs used to model games?
examQuestions.answer: Positions as vertices, moves as edges; backward labelling.

knowledgeCheck.question: In a game graph an edge represents:
A position is winning if some move reaches a losing position.
Is n=3 winning in the 1-or-2 coin game?
Graph vs tree for games.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Graph allows repeated positions; tree duplicates them.

daa-c5-t01.quickRevision: Games as graphs: positions=vertices, moves=edges; winning if a move reaches a losing position; coin game losing at multiples of 3.
daa-c5-t01.problemStatement: Decide whether a position is winning.
daa-c5-t01.approach: Label terminal positions then work backwards.
algorithmSteps: 1. Build graph of positions/moves.
2. Mark terminal positions (lose for player to move).
3. A position is winning if any successor is losing; losing if all successors are winning.
4. Repeat backwards.

daa-c5-t02.title: Undirected Graph
daa-c5-t02.definition: An undirected graph G=(V,E) is a set of vertices and a set of unordered pairs of vertices (edges) where an edge connects two vertices in both directions.
daa-c5-t02.simpleExplanation: Undirected graph me edge dono taraf jaati hai (A–B matlab B–A bhi). Degree, path, cycle, connectivity jaise concepts hote hain.
daa-c5-t02.realLifeAnalogy: A road network with two-way roads.
daa-c5-t02.example: V={A,B,C,D}, E={AB,AC,BD}. deg(A)=2, deg(B)=2, deg(C)=1, deg(D)=1; sum degrees = 6 = 2|E|.
keyPoints: Edge {u,v} unordered; degree = number of incident edges.
Handshake lemma: Σ deg(v)=2|E|.
Complete graph Kₙ has n(n−1)/2 edges.
Connected if a path exists between every pair; tree = connected acyclic.
Representations: adjacency matrix O(V²) space; adjacency list O(V+E).
Path, cycle, connected component.
commonMistakes: Counting an undirected edge twice in |E|.
Using matrix for sparse graphs.

examQuestions.question: Adjacency matrix vs list.
examQuestions.answer: Matrix O(V²) space, O(1) edge check; list O(V+E) space, efficient traversal.

knowledgeCheck.question: Path vs cycle.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Path: sequence of vertices via edges; cycle: path starting and ending at same vertex.

daa-c5-t02.quickRevision: Undirected graph: unordered edges; Σdeg=2|E|; Kₙ has n(n−1)/2 edges; matrix O(V²) vs list O(V+E).

daa-c5-t03.title: Directed Graph
daa-c5-t03.definition: A directed graph (digraph) has edges with direction, each edge (u,v) going from u to v only.
daa-c5-t03.simpleExplanation: Directed graph me edge ka direction hota hai (A→B alag hai B→A se). In-degree, out-degree, strongly connected, DAG jaise concepts important hain.
daa-c5-t03.realLifeAnalogy: One-way streets: you can go from A to B but not back.
daa-c5-t03.example: V={1,2,3}, E={(1,2),(2,3),(3,1)}: a directed cycle; each vertex has in-degree 1 and out-degree 1; strongly connected.
keyPoints: Edge (u,v) ≠ (v,u).
Σ in-degree = Σ out-degree = |E|.
Max edges n(n−1) without self loops.
Strongly connected: every vertex reachable from every other.
DAG: directed acyclic graph (topological ordering exists).
Adjacency list stores only out-neighbours.
commonMistakes: Treating directed edges as undirected.
Assuming every digraph has a topological order (only DAGs).

examQuestions.question: Explain directed graphs and their terms.
examQuestions.answer: Direction, in/out degree, strongly connected, DAG.

examQuestions.question: Max edges in a digraph of n vertices?
examQuestions.answer: n(n−1) (no self-loops).

daa-c5-t03.quickRevision: Digraph: ordered edges; Σin=Σout=|E|; DAG has topological order; max n(n−1) edges.

daa-c5-t04.title: Traversing Graphs
daa-c5-t04.definition: Graph traversal visits every vertex (and edge) of a graph exactly once in a systematic order, using DFS or BFS with a visited marker.
daa-c5-t04.simpleExplanation: Traversal matlab graph ke saare vertices ko ek baar visit karna. Visited array rakhte hain taaki cycle me phase na. Do tareeke: DFS (stack/recursion) aur BFS (queue).
daa-c5-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Exploring a city: either go as deep as possible down one street before returning (DFS) or visit all nearby streets first (BFS).
daa-c5-t04.example: Graph A–B, A–C, B–D, C–E. DFS from A: A,B,D,C,E. BFS from A: A,B,C,D,E.
keyPoints: Mark visited to avoid infinite loops.
Start vertex; for disconnected graphs, restart from unvisited vertices (components).
DFS uses stack/recursion; BFS uses queue.
Time O(V+E) with adjacency list; O(V²) with matrix.
Produces a traversal tree/forest.
Foundation for connectivity, cycle detection, shortest paths.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the visited check.
Not handling disconnected graphs.

examQuestions.question: Explain graph traversal and its types.
examQuestions.answer: DFS and BFS with visited marking and complexity.

examQuestions.question: How count connected components?
examQuestions.answer: Run traversal from each unvisited vertex; count starts.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why mark visited?
knowledgeCheck.answer: To avoid revisiting and infinite loops.

daa-c5-t04.quickRevision: Traversal: visit all vertices once with visited[]; DFS (stack) / BFS (queue); O(V+E); restart for components.
algorithmSteps: 1. Mark all vertices unvisited.
2. For each unvisited vertex v: traverse from v.
3. Mark v visited; explore neighbours not yet visited.

daa-c5-t05.title: Depth First Search
daa-c5-t05.definition: Depth First Search (DFS) explores a graph by going as deep as possible along each branch before backtracking, using recursion or a stack.
daa-c5-t05.simpleExplanation: DFS ek raste pe jitna ho sake andar tak jaata hai, phir wapas aake dusra raasta try karta hai. Stack ya recursion use hota hai.
daa-c5-t05.realLifeAnalogy: Exploring a maze by following one corridor until a dead end, then backing up to try another.
daa-c5-t05.example: Graph edges A–B, A–C, B–D, C–E. DFS(A): visit A → B → D (dead end) → back to A → C → E. Order: A,B,D,C,E.
keyPoints: Uses stack/recursion; discovery and finish times.
Edge types in digraph: tree, back, forward, cross; back edge ⇒ cycle.
Time O(V+E); space O(V).
Applications: cycle detection, topological sort, strongly connected components, maze solving.
Does not guarantee shortest paths.
DFS tree/forest.
commonMistakes: Using DFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs (BFS is right).
Forgetting recursion depth limits.

examQuestions.question: DFS order from A for A–B, A–C, B–D, C–E.
examQuestions.answer: A,B,D,C,E.

examQuestions.question: Write DFS and applications.
examQuestions.answer: Pseudocode, O(V+E), cycle detection, topological sort.

knowledgeCheck.question: A back edge indicates a cycle.
Detect cycle in a directed graph. Method?
DFS vs BFS shortest path.
knowledgeCheck.answer: BFS gives shortest unweighted paths; DFS does not.

daa-c5-t05.quickRevision: DFS: go deep, backtrack; stack/recursion; O(V+E); back edge ⇒ cycle; used in topological sort, SCC.
daa-c5-t05.problemStatement: Visit all vertices reachable from a source.
algorithmSteps: 1. Mark v visited.
2. For each neighbour w of v: if not visited, DFS(w).
3. Record finish time.
daa-c5-t05.pseudocode:
DFS(G)
  for each v: visited[v] ← false
  for each v: if not visited[v] then DFSVisit(v)
DFSVisit(u)
  visited[u] ← true
  for each w in Adj[u] do
    if not visited[w] then DFSVisit(w)
daa-c5-t05.workedExample: A:[B,C], B:[A,D], C:[A,E] → A, B, D, C, E.

daa-c5-t06.title: Breadth First Search
daa-c5-t06.definition: Breadth First Search (BFS) explores a graph level by level from a source using a queue, finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
daa-c5-t06.simpleExplanation: BFS pehle source ke saare nazdeeki neighbours, phir unke neighbours, aise level-by-level visit karta hai. Queue use hoti hai. Unweighted graph me shortest path deta hai.
daa-c5-t06.realLifeAnalogy: Ripples in a pond: the wave reaches near points first, then farther ones.
daa-c5-t06.example: Graph A–B, A–C, B–D, C–E. BFS(A): queue [A] → visit A, enqueue B,C → B (enqueue D) → C (enqueue E) → D → E. Order A,B,C,D,E; distances A0,B1,C1,D2,E2.
keyPoints: Queue-based; level order.
Shortest path (fewest edges) in unweighted graphs.
Time O(V+E); space O(V).
Applications: shortest path, connectivity, bipartite check, level-order.
BFS tree stores parents.
Memory heavy for wide graphs.
commonMistakes: Marking visited when dequeued instead of when enqueued (duplicates).
Using BFS for weighted shortest paths.

examQuestions.question: BFS order and distances from A.
DFS vs BFS.
examQuestions.answer: Stack/deep vs queue/level; BFS gives shortest unweighted paths.

knowledgeCheck.question: BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
Distance of D from A in the example.
BFS vs Dijkstra.
knowledgeCheck.answer: BFS for unweighted; Dijkstra for non-negative weights.

daa-c5-t06.quickRevision: BFS: queue, level order, shortest unweighted paths, O(V+E).
daa-c5-t06.problemStatement: Visit vertices in increasing distance from source.
daa-c5-t06.approach: Process vertices from a FIFO queue.
algorithmSteps: 1. Mark s visited; enqueue s; dist[s]=0.
2. While queue not empty: u=dequeue.
3. For each unvisited neighbour w: mark, dist[w]=dist[u]+1, enqueue.
daa-c5-t06.pseudocode:
BFS(G,s)
  visited[s] ← true; dist[s] ← 0; Enqueue(Q,s)
  while Q not empty do
    u ← Dequeue(Q)
    for each w in Adj[u] do
      if not visited[w] then visited[w] ← true; dist[w] ← dist[u]+1; Enqueue(Q,w)

daa-c5-t07.title: Topological Sort
daa-c5-t07.definition: A topological sort of a directed acyclic graph is a linear ordering of its vertices such that for every edge u→v, u appears before v.
daa-c5-t07.simpleExplanation: Topological sort DAG ke vertices ko aise line me lagata hai ki har edge u→v me u pehle aaye. Jaise courses ka prerequisite order. Kahn's algorithm (in-degree) ya DFS finish time se karte hain.
daa-c5-t07.realLifeAnalogy: Getting dressed: socks before shoes, shirt before tie.
keyPoints: Exists only for DAGs.
Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove vertices with in-degree 0.
DFS method: order by decreasing finish time.
Time O(V+E).
Ordering may not be unique.
If Kahn's cannot remove all vertices, there is a cycle.
commonMistakes: Applying to graphs with cycles.
Thinking the order is unique.

examQuestions.question: Topological order of 5→2,5→0,4→0,4→1,2→3,3→1.
examQuestions.answer: 4,5,2,0,3,1 (one valid answer).

examQuestions.question: How does Kahn's algorithm detect cycles?
examQuestions.answer: If some vertices remain with in-degree >0 when the queue empties.
