knowledgeCheck.question: Kahn vs DFS method.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Kahn uses in-degrees/queue; DFS uses reverse finishing times.

daa-c5-t07.quickRevision: Topological sort: DAG ordering; Kahn (in-degree 0 queue) or DFS reverse finish; O(V+E); cycle ⇒ impossible.
daa-c5-t07.problemStatement: Order vertices of a DAG so all edges go forward.
daa-c5-t07.approach: Repeatedly output a vertex with no remaining incoming edges.
algorithmSteps: 1. Compute in-degree of every vertex.
2. Enqueue vertices with in-degree 0.
3. Dequeue u, output it; reduce in-degree of its neighbours; enqueue those reaching 0.
4. If output count < V, a cycle exists.
daa-c5-t07.pseudocode:
TopoSort(G)
  compute indeg[v]; Q ← vertices with indeg 0
  while Q not empty do
    u ← Dequeue(Q); output u
    for each v in Adj[u] do
      indeg[v] ← indeg[v]−1
      if indeg[v] = 0 then Enqueue(Q,v)

daa-c6-t01.title: Introduction to Backtracking
daa-c6-t01.definition: Backtracking builds a solution incrementally, exploring a state-space tree depth-first and abandoning (backtracking from) any partial solution that cannot lead to a valid complete solution.
daa-c6-t01.simpleExplanation: Backtracking me hum step by step solution banate hain. Agar koi partial solution galat nikle to wahi se wapas aake dusra option try karte hain. Ye smart brute force hai jo bekar branches kaat deta hai.
daa-c6-t01.realLifeAnalogy: Solving a maze: take a path; at a dead end return to the last junction and try another turn.
daa-c6-t01.example: Subset-sum: choose numbers from {3,5,7} to reach 8: include 3, include 5 → sum 8 ✓. If sum exceeds 8, stop that branch (prune) and backtrack.
keyPoints: Depth-first search of the state-space tree.
Constraints (explicit and implicit) decide validity.
Bounding/pruning function kills non-promising nodes.
Promising node: may lead to a solution.
Typical problems: N-Queens, subset sum, graph colouring, Hamiltonian cycle, Sudoku.
Worst case still exponential.
commonMistakes: Not undoing the choice before trying the next option.
Missing a pruning condition so it behaves like brute force.

examQuestions.question: Explain backtracking with an example.
examQuestions.answer: DFS on state-space tree with pruning; N-Queens or subset sum.

examQuestions.question: Backtracking vs brute force.
examQuestions.answer: Backtracking prunes partial solutions early; brute force generates all complete candidates.

knowledgeCheck.question: Sum exceeds target in subset-sum. Action?
Backtracking vs branch & bound.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Backtracking for feasibility; B&B for optimisation using bounds.

daa-c6-t01.quickRevision: Backtracking: DFS on state-space tree, prune non-promising nodes, undo and try next; exponential worst case.
daa-c6-t01.problemStatement: Find solutions satisfying constraints among many candidates.
daa-c6-t01.approach: Extend partial solutions; abandon when constraints fail.
algorithmSteps: 1. Start with an empty partial solution.
2. Try each option for the next component.
3. If the partial solution is promising → recurse.
4. If complete and valid → record; otherwise undo and try the next option.
daa-c6-t01.pseudocode:
Backtrack(k)
  for each choice x for position k do
    if Promising(k, x) then
      X[k] ← x
      if k = n then output X else Backtrack(k+1)

daa-c6-t02.title: Introduction to Branch & Bound
daa-c6-t02.definition: Branch and bound solves optimisation problems by branching into sub-problems and using bounds on the best possible value in each branch to discard branches that cannot beat the best solution found so far.
daa-c6-t02.simpleExplanation: Branch & bound optimization problems ke liye hai. Har node ke liye ek bound nikalte hain (best kitna mil sakta hai). Agar bound abhi tak ke best se kharab hai to us branch ko kaat dete hain.
daa-c6-t02.realLifeAnalogy: Shopping with a budget: if even the best-case total of a basket already exceeds your best deal, stop exploring that basket.
daa-c6-t02.example: 0/1 knapsack: at each node compute an upper bound using the fractional knapsack; if bound ≤ best known value, prune the node.
keyPoints: Branching: split into smaller sub-problems; bounding: estimate best value reachable.
Live node, E-node (being expanded), dead node.
Search strategies: FIFO (BFS), LIFO (DFS), least-cost / best-first with priority queue.
Prune if bound is not better than the incumbent best.
Used for knapsack, TSP, job assignment.
Worst case still exponential, but practical savings are large.
commonMistakes: Using weak bounds that prune nothing.
Pruning with an optimistic bound in the wrong direction.

examQuestions.question: Explain branch and bound.
examQuestions.answer: Branch, bound, prune using incumbent; strategies.

examQuestions.question: Backtracking vs branch & bound.
examQuestions.answer: Backtracking: any feasible solution(s), DFS; B&B: optimal solution with bounds and various search orders.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the incumbent?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Best complete solution found so far.

knowledgeCheck.question: Node bound worse than incumbent. Action?
FIFO vs LIFO B&B.
knowledgeCheck.answer: FIFO uses a queue (BFS-like); LIFO uses a stack (DFS-like).

daa-c6-t02.quickRevision: B&B: branch + bound + prune against incumbent; FIFO/LIFO/least-cost; for optimisation.
daa-c6-t02.problemStatement: Find an optimal solution among many feasible ones.
daa-c6-t02.approach: Compute bounds per node; prune branches that cannot beat the best.
algorithmSteps: 1. Create root; compute its bound.
2. Choose a live node (queue/stack/priority).
3. Branch into children; compute bounds.
4. Prune children whose bound ≤ best (max problem).
5. Update best at feasible leaves; repeat until no live nodes.

daa-c6-t03.title: 0/1 Knapsack Problem (Backtracking / Branch & Bound)
daa-c6-t03.definition: Solving 0/1 knapsack with backtracking or branch and bound explores include/exclude decisions in a state-space tree and prunes nodes whose upper bound cannot beat the best value found.
daa-c6-t03.simpleExplanation: Yahan 0/1 knapsack ko backtracking / branch & bound se solve karte hain: har item ko include ya exclude, aur fractional-knapsack bound se bekar branches kaat dete hain.
daa-c6-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Packing a suitcase item by item: if even with the best possible remaining items you can't beat your best packing so far, stop that attempt.
daa-c6-t03.example: W=10; items (value,weight) sorted by ratio: (40,4),(42,7),(25,5),(12,3). Root bound: 40 + (6/7)·42 = 76. Best complete: items 1+3 → value 65, weight 9. Branch 'exclude item 1' has bound 42+15 = 57 < 65 ⇒ pruned.
keyPoints: Sort items by value/weight descending.
State-space tree: left = include, right = exclude.
Upper bound: fill remaining capacity with fractional items.
Prune if weight > W or bound ≤ best.
Optimal for the example is 65 (items 1 and 3).
Compare with DP O(nW).
commonMistakes: Not sorting by ratio (weak bounds).
Using the bound as the node's value.

examQuestions.question: Solve W=10, items (40,4),(42,7),(25,5),(12,3) by B&B.
examQuestions.answer: Optimal 65 with items 1 and 3.

examQuestions.question: How is the upper bound computed?
examQuestions.answer: Greedy fractional knapsack on remaining items.

knowledgeCheck.question: Items should be sorted by value/weight ratio.
Prune when?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Bound ≤ best known value or weight exceeds capacity.

knowledgeCheck.question: B&B vs DP for knapsack.
knowledgeCheck.answer: B&B prunes tree; DP fills O(nW) table.

daa-c6-t03.quickRevision: 0/1 knapsack B&B: sort by ratio, include/exclude tree, fractional upper bound, prune; example optimum 65.
daa-c6-t03.problemStatement: Maximise value with capacity W, whole items only.
daa-c6-t03.approach: Search include/exclude tree with fractional upper bounds.
algorithmSteps: 1. Sort by v/w descending.
2. At each node compute weight, value and upper bound.
3. If weight>W or bound ≤ best → prune.
4. Branch include/exclude; update best at leaves.
daa-c6-t03.workedExample: Root ub=76. Include 1 (w4,v40) ub=76. Include 3 → w9,v65 (best=65). Exclude 1: ub=57 <65 pruned.
daa-c6-t03.timeComplexity: Exponential worst case; typically far fewer nodes

daa-c6-t04.title: N-Queens Problem
daa-c6-t04.definition: The N-Queens problem places N queens on an N×N chessboard so that no two queens attack each other (same row, column or diagonal), solved by backtracking.
daa-c6-t04.simpleExplanation: N×N board par N queens aise rakhni hain ki koi ek doosre ko attack na kare. Row by row queen rakhte hain; conflict aaye to piche jaake position badalte hain.
daa-c6-t04.realLifeAnalogy: Seating guests who dislike sitting in line of sight with each other: place one, check conflicts, move if needed.
daa-c6-t04.example: 4-Queens: row1 col2, row2 col4, row3 col1, row4 col3 → solution (2,4,1,3). Another is (3,1,4,2).
keyPoints: One queen per row; track column of each queen X[i].
Conflict if same column or |X[i]−X[j]| = |i−j| (diagonal).
Backtrack when no safe column in a row.
4-Queens has 2 solutions; 8-Queens has 92 (12 distinct).
Worst-case O(n!) but pruning cuts it hugely.
Symmetry can halve the work.
commonMistakes: Forgetting diagonal check.
Not undoing a placement on backtrack.

examQuestions.question: Explain N-Queens using backtracking.
examQuestions.answer: Row-wise placement, safe check, backtrack on failure.

knowledgeCheck.question: Row has no safe column. Action?
Brute force vs backtracking for N-Queens.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Brute force tries all placements; backtracking prunes unsafe partial placements.

daa-c6-t04.quickRevision: N-Queens: place row by row; safe if different column and |Δcol|≠|Δrow|; backtrack; 4-Queens (2,4,1,3).
daa-c6-t04.problemStatement: Place N non-attacking queens on an N×N board.
daa-c6-t04.approach: Place one queen per row, pruning conflicting columns/diagonals.
algorithmSteps: 1. For row k=1..N try each column i.
2. If Place(k,i) is safe set X[k]=i.
3. If k=N print solution else recurse on k+1.
4. If no column works, backtrack.
daa-c6-t04.pseudocode:
Place(k,i)
  for j ← 1 to k−1 do
    if X[j]=i or |X[j]−i| = |j−k| then return false
  return true
NQueens(k,n)
  for i ← 1 to n do
    if Place(k,i) then
      X[k] ← i
      if k=n then print X else NQueens(k+1,n)

daa-c6-t05.title: Travelling Salesman Problem
daa-c6-t05.definition: The travelling salesman problem (TSP) asks for the shortest tour that visits every city exactly once and returns to the start; it is NP-hard and can be solved exactly by dynamic programming (Held–Karp) or branch and bound.
daa-c6-t05.simpleExplanation: TSP me salesman ko saare cities ek baar visit karke wapas start par aana hai, sabse kam distance me. Brute force (n−1)! hai; DP O(n²2ⁿ); branch & bound me reduced cost matrix se lower bound nikalte hain.
daa-c6-t05.realLifeAnalogy: A delivery rider planning the shortest loop through all customers' homes and back to the shop.
daa-c6-t05.example: Distances A–B 10, A–C 15, A–D 20, B–C 35, B–D 25, C–D 30. Best tour A→B→D→C→A = 10+25+30+15 = 80. Row/column reduction gives root lower bound 70 ≤ 80.
keyPoints: NP-hard; decision version is NP-complete.
Brute force: (n−1)! tours.
Held–Karp DP: O(n²·2ⁿ) time, O(n·2ⁿ) space.
Branch & bound: reduce cost matrix (subtract row/column minima) to get a lower bound.
Approximation: nearest neighbour, 2-approx for metric TSP via MST.
Applications: logistics, circuit drilling, DNA sequencing.
ifYouKnow: Compute the optimal tour for 4 cities.
Compute a lower bound by reduction.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to return to the start city.
Assuming greedy nearest neighbour is optimal.

examQuestions.question: Optimal tour for the 4-city matrix.
examQuestions.answer: A-B-D-C-A (or reverse), length 80.

examQuestions.question: Root lower bound by matrix reduction.
examQuestions.answer: Row minima 10+10+15+20=55, column reductions 0+0+5+10 = 15 ⇒ 70.

examQuestions.question: Why is TSP hard?
examQuestions.answer: Number of tours grows factorially; NP-hard.

knowledgeCheck.question: Tour A-B-C-D-A length for the example.
DP vs B&B for TSP.
knowledgeCheck.answer: DP exact with exponential table; B&B prunes using lower bounds.

daa-c6-t05.quickRevision: TSP: shortest Hamiltonian tour; brute force (n−1)!; Held–Karp O(n²2ⁿ); B&B with reduced matrix; example 80 (LB 70).
daa-c6-t05.problemStatement: Find the minimum-cost tour visiting all cities once and returning to start.
daa-c6-t05.approach: Branch & bound using a reduced cost matrix as lower bound (or DP over subsets).
algorithmSteps: 1. Reduce the cost matrix: subtract row minima then column minima; sum = lower bound.
2. Branch on including/excluding an edge; set the corresponding row/column to ∞ and re-reduce.
3. Bound = parent bound + reduction cost.
4. Expand the least-bound live node; prune if bound ≥ best tour.
5. Stop when a complete tour with minimum bound is found.
daa-c6-t05.workedExample: Reduced matrix rows: A[∞,0,5,10], B[0,∞,25,15], C[0,20,∞,15], D[0,5,10,∞]; column reductions C:5, D:10; LB=55+15=70; optimal tour 80.

daa-c7-t01.title: Introduction to String Matching
daa-c7-t01.definition: String matching finds all occurrences (valid shifts) of a pattern P of length m inside a text T of length n.
daa-c7-t01.simpleExplanation: Text me pattern kahan kahan aata hai ye dhundna string matching hai. Algorithms: naive, Rabin–Karp, KMP, finite automata — sabka time/preprocessing alag hota hai.
daa-c7-t01.realLifeAnalogy: Ctrl+F in a document: finding every place where a word appears.
daa-c7-t01.example: T=ABABCABAB, P=ABAB: P occurs with shifts s=0 and s=5.
keyPoints: Text T[1..n], pattern P[1..m], alphabet Σ.
Shift s valid if T[s+1..s+m]=P.
Naive: O((n−m+1)m).
Rabin–Karp: hashing, average O(n+m).
KMP: prefix function, O(n+m).
Finite automaton: preprocessing O(m|Σ|), matching O(n).
commonMistakes: Confusing shift with index of last matching char.
Ignoring preprocessing cost.

examQuestions.question: Explain string matching problem and algorithms.
examQuestions.answer: Definition, shifts, algorithms and complexities.

examQuestions.question: Valid shifts of ABAB in ABABCABAB.
examQuestions.answer: 0 and 5.

knowledgeCheck.question: Number of shifts to try naively for n=9, m=4.

daa-c7-t01.quickRevision: String matching: find valid shifts of P in T; naive O(nm), Rabin–Karp avg O(n+m), KMP O(n+m), automaton O(n).
daa-c7-t01.problemStatement: Find all shifts s where P occurs in T.

daa-c7-t02.title: Naive String Matching
daa-c7-t02.definition: The naive algorithm checks, for every possible shift of the pattern, whether the pattern matches the text there by comparing character by character.
daa-c7-t02.simpleExplanation: Naive method me pattern ko text par har position par rakh ke compare karte hain. Simple hai par worst case me slow (O(nm)).
daa-c7-t02.realLifeAnalogy: Sliding a stencil across a page and checking at each position whether the letters fit.
daa-c7-t02.example: T=ABABCABAB, P=ABAB: shift 0 matches; shifts 1–4 fail early; shift 5 matches ⇒ shifts {0,5}.
keyPoints: Tries all n−m+1 shifts.
Worst case O((n−m+1)·m) e.g. T=AAAA…A, P=AAAB.
Best case O(n) when the first characters mismatch quickly.
No preprocessing; O(1) extra space.
Simple but wastes information from previous comparisons.
Basis for improved algorithms.
commonMistakes: Thinking naive is always O(n).
Off-by-one in the shift range.

examQuestions.answer: Matches at shifts 0 and 5.

examQuestions.answer: Loop shifts, compare; O((n−m+1)m).

knowledgeCheck.question: Worst-case input type?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Repetitive text and pattern like AAAA… and AAAB.

knowledgeCheck.question: Naive vs Rabin–Karp.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Naive compares characters directly; Rabin–Karp compares hashes first.

daa-c7-t02.quickRevision: Naive: try all n−m+1 shifts comparing chars; worst O((n−m+1)m); no preprocessing.
daa-c7-t02.problemStatement: Find all occurrences of P in T.
algorithmSteps: 1. For s = 0 to n−m.
2. Compare P[1..m] with T[s+1..s+m].
3. If all match, report shift s.
daa-c7-t02.pseudocode:
NaiveMatch(T,P)
  n ← |T|; m ← |P|
  for s ← 0 to n−m do
    if T[s+1..s+m] = P then print "shift" s
daa-c7-t02.workedExample: T=ABABCABAB,P=ABAB: s=0 ✓; s=1 B≠A; s=2 ABC≠ABA B? mismatch at 4th char; s=3 ✗; s=4 ✗; s=5 ✓.

daa-c7-t03.title: Rabin-Karp Algorithm
daa-c7-t03.definition: Rabin–Karp compares a hash of the pattern with rolling hashes of text windows and checks characters only when hashes match.
daa-c7-t03.simpleExplanation: Rabin–Karp me pattern ka hash nikalte hain aur text ki har window ka hash 'rolling' tareeke se update karte hain. Hash match ho tabhi characters compare karte hain. Kabhi kabhi spurious hit bhi hota hai.
daa-c7-t03.realLifeAnalogy: Comparing fingerprints first, and only comparing faces when the fingerprints match.
daa-c7-t03.example: T=3141592653, P=26, base 10, modulus q=11. hash(P)=26 mod 11=4. Windows: 31→9, 14→3, 41→8, 15→4 (spurious), 59→4 (spurious), 92→4 (spurious), 26→4 (real match at shift 6), 65→10, 53→9.
keyPoints: Rolling hash: t_{s+1}=(d·(t_s − T[s+1]·h) + T[s+m+1]) mod q, h=d^{m−1} mod q.
Hash equal ⇒ verify characters (spurious hits possible).
Average/expected O(n+m); worst O(nm) with many spurious hits.
Good for multiple pattern search.
Choose a large prime q.
Preprocessing Θ(m).
commonMistakes: Skipping the verification step on a hash match.
Using a small modulus causing many spurious hits.

examQuestions.question: T=3141592653, P=26, q=11: find the match and spurious hits.
examQuestions.answer: Spurious at shifts 3,4,5; true match at shift 6.

examQuestions.question: What is a spurious hit?
examQuestions.answer: Hash equal but strings differ.

knowledgeCheck.question: Hash match guarantees a pattern match.
Rabin–Karp vs naive.
knowledgeCheck.answer: Rabin–Karp filters with hashes; naive compares directly.

daa-c7-t03.quickRevision: Rabin–Karp: rolling hash mod q; verify on hash match; avg O(n+m), worst O(nm); spurious hits.
daa-c7-t03.problemStatement: Find P in T using hashing.
daa-c7-t03.approach: Compare window hashes with the pattern hash; verify on equality.
algorithmSteps: 1. Compute h=d^{m−1} mod q, hash of P and first window.
2. For each shift: if hash equal, verify characters.
3. Update the hash for the next window with the rolling formula.
daa-c7-t03.pseudocode:
RabinKarp(T,P,d,q)
  h ← d^(m−1) mod q; p ← 0; t ← 0
  for i ← 1 to m do p ← (d·p+P[i]) mod q; t ← (d·t+T[i]) mod q
  for s ← 0 to n−m do
    if p = t and T[s+1..s+m] = P then print s
    if s < n−m then t ← (d·(t − T[s+1]·h) + T[s+m+1]) mod q
daa-c7-t03.workedExample: Windows of 3141592653 (length 2) mod 11: 9,3,8,4,4,4,4,10,9; hash(P)=4 → verify at 3,4,5 (fail) and 6 (match).

daa-c7-t04.title: Knuth-Morris-Pratt Algorithm
daa-c7-t04.definition: The Knuth–Morris–Pratt (KMP) algorithm matches a pattern in O(n+m) time by using a prefix (failure) function to avoid re-examining text characters after a mismatch.
daa-c7-t04.simpleExplanation: KMP mismatch hone par text me peeche nahi jaata. Pattern ka prefix function π batata hai ki pattern ke andar kitna prefix pehle se match ho chuka hai, isliye pattern ko smartly shift karta hai.
daa-c7-t04.realLifeAnalogy: When you misread a word while reading aloud, you don't start the sentence over; you resume from the part you already know matches.
daa-c7-t04.example: P=ABABAC: π=[0,0,1,2,3,0]. T=ABABABAC: after matching ABABA, mismatch at B vs C → q=π[4]=3; then B matches, A, C ⇒ full match at shift 2.
keyPoints: Prefix function π[q]: length of the longest proper prefix of P[1..q] that is also a suffix.
Preprocessing Θ(m); matching Θ(n).
Text pointer never moves backward.
On mismatch set q ← π[q−1].
Total Θ(n+m).
Good for long patterns and streaming text.
commonMistakes: Setting wrong fallback index (off-by-one).
Thinking π stores positions in the text.

examQuestions.question: Run KMP on T=ABABABAC with P=ABABAC.
examQuestions.answer: Match at shift 2.

examQuestions.question: Why is KMP O(n+m)?
examQuestions.answer: Text pointer never decreases and q decreases at most as often as it increases.

knowledgeCheck.question: KMP moves the text pointer backwards.
What is the prefix function?
knowledgeCheck.answer: Longest proper prefix that is also a suffix for each prefix of P.

knowledgeCheck.question: KMP vs naive.
knowledgeCheck.answer: KMP avoids re-comparing; naive restarts from the next shift.

daa-c7-t04.quickRevision: KMP: prefix function π (longest proper prefix=suffix), mismatch → q=π[q−1]; Θ(n+m).
daa-c7-t04.problemStatement: Find P in T without backing up the text pointer.
daa-c7-t04.approach: Precompute π; on mismatch fall back using π.
algorithmSteps: 1. Compute π for P.
2. q=0; for i in T: while q>0 and P[q+1]≠T[i]: q=π[q].
4. If q=m: report match at i−m; q=π[q].
daa-c7-t04.pseudocode:
ComputePrefix(P)
  π[1] ← 0; k ← 0
  for q ← 2 to m do
    while k>0 and P[k+1]≠P[q] do k ← π[k]
    if P[k+1]=P[q] then k ← k+1
    π[q] ← k
KMP(T,P)
  q ← 0
  for i ← 1 to n do
    while q>0 and P[q+1]≠T[i] do q ← π[q]
    if P[q+1]=T[i] then q ← q+1
    if q=m then print i−m; q ← π[q]
daa-c7-t04.workedExample: P=ABABAC π=[0,0,1,2,3,0]. T=ABABABAC: q:1,2,3,4,5 → mismatch → q=3 → 4 → 5 → 6=m ⇒ shift 2.

daa-c7-t05.title: String Matching using Finite Automata
daa-c7-t05.definition: A string-matching automaton is a DFA that reads the text one character at a time and enters its accepting state exactly when a pattern occurrence ends.
daa-c7-t05.simpleExplanation: Pattern ke liye ek DFA banate hain jisme state i matlab 'pattern ke pehle i chars match ho chuke'. Text ek baar padhte hain; accepting state m aaye to match mil gaya. Matching O(n).
daa-c7-t05.realLifeAnalogy: A turnstile that moves forward one step for each correct letter and resets or falls back for wrong ones.
daa-c7-t05.example: P=ABA over {A,B}: δ(0,A)=1, δ(0,B)=0; δ(1,A)=1, δ(1,B)=2; δ(2,A)=3, δ(2,B)=0; δ(3,A)=1, δ(3,B)=2. Text ABABA: states 0→1→2→3 (match ends at 3rd char) →2→3 (match). Shifts 0 and 2.
keyPoints: States 0..m; accepting state m.
δ(q,a)=length of the longest prefix of P that is a suffix of P_q a.
Matching takes Θ(n) after building the automaton.
Preprocessing O(m|Σ|) (efficient) or O(m³|Σ|) naive.
Transition table size (m+1)|Σ|.
KMP is a space-efficient version of this idea.
commonMistakes: Forgetting transitions from the accepting state.
Wrong fallback in δ.

examQuestions.question: Build the automaton for P=ABA over {A,B} and run on ABABA.
examQuestions.answer: Table as above; matches end at positions 3 and 5.

examQuestions.question: Automaton vs KMP.
examQuestions.answer: Automaton stores a full transition table (O(m|Σ|)); KMP stores only π (O(m)).

daa-c7-t05.quickRevision: String-matching DFA: states 0..m, δ(q,a)=longest prefix of P that is suffix of P_q a; match at state m; Θ(n).
daa-c7-t05.problemStatement: Find P in T using a DFA.
algorithmSteps: 1. Build δ for states 0..m and each symbol a.
2. q=0; for each text char T[i]: q=δ(q,T[i]).
3. If q=m, report match ending at i.
daa-c7-t05.pseudocode:
FA-Matcher(T,δ,m)
  q ← 0
  for i ← 1 to n do
    q ← δ(q, T[i])
    if q = m then print i−m

daa-c7-t06.title: Introduction to NP Completeness
daa-c7-t06.definition: NP-completeness classifies decision problems that are in NP and at least as hard as every problem in NP (via polynomial-time reductions), so a fast algorithm for one would give fast algorithms for all.
daa-c7-t06.simpleExplanation: Kuch problems ke liye aaj tak koi fast (polynomial) algorithm nahi mila. NP-complete woh hard problems hain jo NP me hote hain aur har NP problem unme reduce ho sakta hai. Ek ka fast solution mil jaye to sab ka mil jayega.
daa-c7-t06.realLifeAnalogy: A set of locks that are all opened by one master key: if you find it for one, you have it for all.
daa-c7-t06.example: SAT was the first proven NP-complete problem (Cook–Levin). 3-SAT ≤p Clique ≤p Vertex Cover; Hamiltonian cycle and TSP (decision) are NP-complete.
keyPoints: Decision problem: answer yes/no.
Reduction A ≤p B: transform instances of A to B in polynomial time.
NP-hard: every NP problem reduces to it (need not be in NP).
NP-complete = NP ∩ NP-hard.
Cook–Levin: SAT is NP-complete.
Proving NP-completeness: show in NP + reduce a known NP-complete problem to it.
commonMistakes: Reducing in the wrong direction.
Confusing NP-hard with NP-complete.

examQuestions.question: NP-hard vs NP-complete.

daa-c7-t07.title: P Class Problems
daa-c7-t07.definition: The class P contains decision problems that can be solved by a deterministic algorithm in polynomial time.
daa-c7-t07.simpleExplanation: P class me wo problems aate hain jinhe normal (deterministic) algorithm polynomial time me solve kar leta hai, jaise sorting, shortest path, MST. Inhe efficiently solvable maana jata hai.
daa-c7-t07.realLifeAnalogy: Tasks you can finish in reasonable time as the problem grows, like sorting a bigger list.
daa-c7-t07.example: Shortest path (Dijkstra), MST (Kruskal), sorting, GCD, checking if a graph is connected, and primality testing (AKS) are in P.
keyPoints: Polynomial time: O(nᵏ) for some constant k.
P is closed under union, intersection, complement and concatenation.
P ⊆ NP.
Considered 'tractable' or efficiently solvable.
Examples: sorting, searching, BFS/DFS, MST, shortest paths, matching.
Polynomial in input length (not value): knapsack DP is pseudo-polynomial.
commonMistakes: Calling O(2ⁿ) polynomial.
Assuming pseudo-polynomial means polynomial.

daa-c7-t08.title: NP Class Problems
daa-c7-t08.definition: The class NP contains decision problems whose 'yes' answers can be verified in polynomial time given a certificate (equivalently, solvable in polynomial time by a non-deterministic machine).
daa-c7-t08.simpleExplanation: NP me wo problems hain jinka answer (certificate) mil jaye to uski sahi hona polynomial time me check ho sakta hai. Solve karna hard ho sakta hai par verify easy.
daa-c7-t08.realLifeAnalogy: A Sudoku: finding the solution is hard, but checking a filled grid is easy.
daa-c7-t08.example: Hamiltonian cycle: given a proposed cycle (certificate), check in O(n) that it visits every vertex once. Subset sum: given a subset, add numbers and compare with target.
keyPoints: Certificate/witness verified in polynomial time.
Non-deterministic polynomial time (NP).
P ⊆ NP; whether P = NP is open.
Examples: SAT, subset sum, clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian cycle, TSP (decision).
NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP.
Co-NP: complements of NP problems.
ifYouKnow: State the P vs NP problem.
commonMistakes: Thinking NP means 'not polynomial'; it means non-deterministic polynomial.
Confusing finding with verifying.

daa-c7-t09.title: Hamiltonian Cycle
daa-c7-t09.definition: A Hamiltonian cycle in a graph is a cycle that visits every vertex exactly once and returns to the start; deciding whether one exists is NP-complete.
daa-c7-t09.simpleExplanation: Hamiltonian cycle me har vertex ko ek hi baar visit karke start par wapas aana hota hai. Existence check NP-complete hai; backtracking se try karte hain.
daa-c7-t09.realLifeAnalogy: A postman who must visit every house exactly once and end where he started (houses, not roads — unlike Euler).
daa-c7-t09.example: Graph 4-cycle A–B–C–D–A has a Hamiltonian cycle A→B→C→D→A. A star graph (center with three leaves) has none.
keyPoints: NP-complete decision problem.
Verifying a given cycle takes O(n).
Backtracking: build path, check edge and not-visited, close the cycle: O(n!) worst.
Held–Karp DP: O(n²2ⁿ).
Reduces to TSP: HC ≤p TSP (weights 1 for edges, 2 for non-edges).
Euler cycle (every edge once) is in P — different problem.
ifYouKnow: Check a graph for HC by backtracking.
commonMistakes: Confusing Hamiltonian (vertices) with Eulerian (edges).
Assuming a simple degree rule decides it.

knowledgeCheck.answer: Hamiltonian: vertices once (NP-complete); Eulerian: edges once (polynomial).

daa-c7-t09.quickRevision: Hamiltonian cycle: visit every vertex once & return; NP-complete; verify O(n); backtracking O(n!); reduces to TSP.
daa-c7-t09.problemStatement: Does graph G have a cycle visiting every vertex exactly once?
daa-c7-t09.approach: Backtracking path construction with visited checks.
algorithmSteps: 1. Fix start vertex v0; path=[v0].
2. For position k try a vertex adjacent to the previous one and not yet used.
3. If k=n and last vertex is adjacent to v0 → cycle found.
4. Otherwise backtrack.
daa-c7-t09.pseudocode:
HamCycle(k)
  repeat
    NextVertex(k)
    if x[k]=0 then return
    if k=n then print x
    else HamCycle(k+1)
  until false
daa-c7-t09.workedExample: 4-cycle A–B–C–D–A: path A,B,C,D and edge D–A closes it ⇒ Hamiltonian cycle.
